shabbat-10b-5-5.note: Rav Hisda was holding two of the priestly gifts from an ox and announced he would give them to anyone who told him a new teaching of Rav. Rava bar Mehasseya told him Rav's teaching that one who gives a gift must let the recipient know, and Rav Hisda gave him the gifts. Rava bar Mehasseya asked whether Rav's teachings were really so dear to him, and Rav Hisda said yes. Rava bar Mehasseya then quoted another saying of Rav: fine wool is precious to those who wear it. Rav Hisda said he liked this second saying even more, and had he held another gift he would have given that too.
shabbat-10b-5-5.why: The Gemara has just cited, through Rava bar Mehasseya, Rav's ruling that a giver must inform the recipient, and worked through an objection to it; this story shows Rava bar Mehasseya first telling that ruling to Rav Hisda.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: A Sage who offered priestly gifts to anyone who brought him a new teaching of Rav.

people.name: Rava bar Mehasseya
people.about: The Sage who told Rav Hisda two teachings of Rav and received the gifts.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The earlier Sage whose teachings Rav Hisda cherished.

terms.term: gifts of the priesthood from an ox
terms.meaning: Portions of a slaughtered animal that the Torah assigns to a priest. Here Rav Hisda, who held them, offered them as a reward for a new teaching.

shabbat-11a-6-6.note: Rav Yehoshua son of Rav Idi visited the house of Rav Ashi, and they prepared a choice calf for him and asked him to eat. He said he was fasting. They asked whether he did not accept Rav Yehuda's ruling that a person may postpone a fast and make it up another day. He answered that it was a fast for a dream, and quoted the teachings that a fast works against a bad dream like fire on chaff, that it must be on the same day, and that it is allowed even on Shabbat.
shabbat-11a-6-6.why: The Gemara has just quoted Rav's teaching that fasting counters a bad dream, with Rav Hisda's and Rav Yosef's additions; the story shows a Sage relying on exactly those teachings to refuse a meal.

people.name: Rav Yehoshua, son of Rav Idi
people.about: A visitor at Rav Ashi's house who declined the meal because he was fasting over a dream.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The host at whose house a calf was prepared for the guest.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage whose ruling that a fast can be borrowed and repaid later is quoted to the guest.

terms.meaning: A calf whose meat was considered especially fine; preparing one was a mark of honor for a guest.
A fast undertaken after a frightening dream, believed to cancel its bad omen. Unlike other fasts it cannot be postponed to another day.

shabbat-12b-4-4.note: Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha said he could read by lamplight on Shabbat without tilting the lamp to adjust the wick. Once he read and found himself about to tilt it, and he said, how great are the words of the Sages who forbade reading by lamplight. Rabbi Natan tells it differently: he read and actually tilted it, then wrote in his notebook, "I, Yishmael ben Elisha, read and tilted a lamp on Shabbat; when the Temple is rebuilt I will bring a fat sin-offering."
shabbat-12b-4-4.why: Rava has ruled that an important person may read by lamplight because he would not handle a lamp; the Gemara objects with this story, and Rabbi Abba answers that Rabbi Yishmael was different, since in Torah study he behaved like an ordinary man.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha
people.about: A Sage who claimed he could read by lamplight on Shabbat without adjusting the wick, and either nearly did or did.

people.name: Rabbi Natan
people.about: A Sage who gives a different account of what Rabbi Yishmael did.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Rules that an important person may read by lamplight on Shabbat.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Explains why Rabbi Yishmael's case does not refute Rava.

terms.meaning: Tilting an oil lamp so the oil reaches the wick and burns brighter. On Shabbat this counts as kindling, which is forbidden, so the Sages barred reading by lamplight in case one does it absent-mindedly.
An animal sacrifice brought in the Temple to atone for breaking a law by mistake.
A collection of early rabbinic teachings from the same era as the Mishna, often quoted in the Gemara.

shabbat-13a-10-10.note: A student who had studied much Mishna and Bible and served Torah scholars died at half his days. His widow carried his phylacteries around the synagogues and study halls, asking how the Torah could promise long life to its students when her husband died young, and no one answered her. Eliyahu tells that he stayed at her house and asked how her husband behaved during her menstrual period. She said he never touched her even with his little finger, but in the clean days that followed, while she was still counting, he ate and drank with her and slept beside her with bodily contact, without thinking of relations. Eliyahu said, blessed is the Omnipresent who killed him, for he showed no regard for the Torah. Later Sages said they shared one bed without contact, or with a garment between them.
shabbat-13a-10-10.why: The Gemara has just cited a teaching that a man may not lie even fully clothed beside his wife while she is menstruating, against Rabbi Pedat's view that only actual relations are forbidden; this teaching of the school of Eliyahu supports the stricter view.

people.name: Eliyahu
people.about: The narrator of the account, who stayed with the widow and gave her the explanation for her husband's death.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: A Sage who came from the Land of Israel to Babylonia and said the couple slept in one bed without contact.

people.name: Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef
people.about: A Sage quoted in the Land of Israel as saying a garment separated the husband and wife.

terms.meaning: Tefillin: small leather boxes holding Torah verses, worn on the arm and head during weekday morning prayer. The widow carried her husband's as a sign of his piety.
After a menstrual period ends, a woman counts seven clean days, checking with white cloths, before immersing. Until then the prohibition on her husband still applies.
A collection of teachings attributed to the prophet Elijah, who in rabbinic tradition visits and teaches the Sages.

shabbat-13b-7-7.note: Rav Yehuda reports in Rav's name: Hananya ben Hizkiya is remembered for good, because without him the book of Ezekiel would have been suppressed, since parts of it contradict the Torah. Three hundred jugs of oil were brought up to him, and he sat in his upper room and interpreted the book until the contradictions were resolved.
shabbat-13b-7-7.why: The mishna has named the upper room of Hananya ben Hizkiya ben Garon, where the Sages issued eighteen decrees, and the Gemara has just credited him and his circle with writing Megillat Taanit; this is a second thing he is remembered for.

people.name: Hananya ben Hizkiya
people.about: A Sage who, shut away in his upper room, reconciled the book of Ezekiel with the Torah.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who reports this teaching in Rav's name.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The earlier Sage whose praise of Hananya ben Hizkiya Rav Yehuda passes on.

terms.meaning: Withdrawn from public use and kept out of the books read as Scripture. The Sages considered doing this to Ezekiel because some of its laws seemed to contradict the Torah.
A room on the roof of a house, often used for study and meetings of the Sages.

shabbat-17a-5-5.note: Shammai and Hillel disagreed over whether grapes harvested for the winepress can become ritually impure. Hillel challenged Shammai: why harvest grapes in purity but not olives? Shammai answered that if Hillel provoked him, he would decree impurity on olives too. A sword was stuck into the study hall and it was announced that anyone could enter but no one could leave. That day Hillel sat bowed before Shammai like a student, and the Gemara says it was as hard for Israel as the day the Golden Calf was made. Shammai and Hillel issued the decree and the people did not accept it; their students later issued it and the people accepted it.
shabbat-17a-5-5.why: The Gemara is counting the eighteen decrees the Sages passed on one famous day and needs to complete the tally. The decree about harvested grapes is given as another of the eighteen; afterward the Gemara asks what the reason for that decree was.

people.name: Hillel
people.about: Head of the Sages in his day; here he argued against the decree and was forced to sit before Shammai like a student.

people.name: Shammai
people.about: Hillel's colleague and opponent, who held that harvested grapes become susceptible to impurity and threatened to extend the decree to olives.

terms.meaning: In Jewish purity law, food can only become ritually impure after it has been moistened by certain liquids. The question is whether juice seeping from grapes during harvest counts.
Using ritually pure vessels and hands, so that the produce stays pure.
The idol the Israelites made in the desert (Exodus 32), remembered as one of the worst days in the nation's history.

shabbat-19a-10-10.note: Abaye gave a dyed garment to a launderer and asked what he would charge. The launderer asked the same price as for a white garment. Abaye told him the Sages had already anticipated him. Abaye also advised that anyone giving clothes to a launderer should measure them when handing them over and when taking them back: if longer, he has stretched and spoiled them; if shorter, he has shrunk them.
shabbat-19a-10-10.why: The Gemara has just inferred from Rabban Gamliel's household custom that white garments are harder to launder than colored ones; Abaye uses that very teaching to refuse the launderer's price.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who refused to pay a launderer the white-garment price for a dyed garment.

shabbat-19b-4-4.note: A student in the town of Harta De'argiz issued a ruling that followed Rabbi Shimon, and Rav Hamnuna excommunicated him. The Gemara asks why, since the law does follow Rabbi Shimon, and answers that the town was Rav's place, so the student should not have ruled against Rav there. The Gemara then mentions two students rescuing belongings from a fire on Shabbat: one carried a single vessel at a time, the other four or five at once.
shabbat-19b-4-4.why: The Gemara has just set out the dispute between Rav, who forbids using set-aside items on Shabbat, and Shmuel, who permits them, matching an earlier dispute of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon; the student's ruling was on that question, given in the town where Rav's ruling held.

people.name: Rav Hamnuna
people.about: A Sage who excommunicated a student for ruling in Rav's town against Rav's view.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: An earlier Sage whose lenient view the student followed.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage whose town it was, and whose stricter view the student's ruling went against.

terms.meaning: Placed under a ban by a Sage, so that the community keeps its distance from the person until he submits.
A town under a particular Sage's authority. Even where the law is lenient, a student may not publicly rule against the local master there; it is an act of disrespect.

shabbat-20b-10-10.note: Ravin and Abaye were walking in the valley of Tamrurita and saw some willow trees. Ravin told Abaye that this was the idan the mishna speaks of. Abaye objected that it was just wood. Ravin peeled off the bark and showed him the wool-like fibers between the bark and the trunk.
shabbat-20b-10-10.why: The Gemara is going through the mishna's list of materials that may not be used as wicks for the Shabbat lamp, identifying each one; just before, Ravin and Abaye identified another item on the list.

people.name: Ravin
people.about: A Sage who identified the willow as the mishna's idan and proved it by peeling the bark.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Ravin's companion on the walk, who doubted that wood could make a wick.

terms.meaning: One of the materials the mishna forbids as a wick for the Shabbat lamp because it does not burn well; the Gemara identifies it as willow fiber.
The early collection of Jewish law that the Gemara comments on line by line.

shabbat-21b-9-9.note: The Sages taught that the eight days of Hanukkah begin on the twenty-fifth of Kislev, and that no one may eulogize or fast on them. When the Greeks entered the Sanctuary, they defiled all its oils. When the Hasmonean dynasty overpowered and defeated them, they searched and found only one cruse of oil still bearing the High Priest's seal, with enough to light the candelabrum for a single day. A miracle happened and they lit from it for eight days. The following year these days were fixed as festive days of praise and thanksgiving.
shabbat-21b-9-9.why: The Gemara has been laying out how the Hanukkah lights are kindled, where the lamp is placed and when another light is needed; it then stops to ask what Hanukkah is, and this account is its answer.

terms.meaning: An ancient list of days of deliverance on which fasting and eulogies were forbidden; the Gemara quotes its entry for Hanukkah.
The priestly family, known also as the Maccabees, who led the revolt against the Greek rulers and then ruled Judea.
The inner hall of the Temple in Jerusalem, where the candelabrum (menorah) stood and was lit each day with pure olive oil.
A set of joyful psalms of praise recited on festivals.

shabbat-23b-3-3.note: Rav Huna taught that one who is regular about lighting lamps will have sons who are Torah scholars. Rav Huna used to pass by the door of Rabbi Avin the carpenter and saw that he lit many lamps; he said two great men would come from that house, and Rav Idi bar Avin and Rav Hiyya bar Avin came from it. Rav Hisda likewise passed by the family home of Rav Sheizvi, saw many lamps lit there, and said a great man would come from it; Rav Sheizvi did.
shabbat-23b-3-3.why: The Gemara has just set the order of priority among the Shabbat lamp, the Hanukkah lamp and the wine for kiddush; Rav Huna's teaching on the reward for lighting lamps, and the two cases that bear it out, follow from that discussion.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage who taught that lighting lamps earns sons who are scholars, and foresaw great men from Rabbi Avin's house.

people.name: Rabbi Avin the carpenter
people.about: A man who lit many lamps; his sons became the Sages Rav Idi and Rav Hiyya.

people.name: Rav Idi bar Avin
people.about: Son of Rabbi Avin the carpenter, one of the two great men Rav Huna foresaw.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: A Sage who foresaw that a great man would come from Rav Sheizvi's family home.

people.name: Rav Sheizvi
people.about: The great man who came from the household where Rav Hisda saw many lamps lit.

terms.meaning: A small parchment scroll with Torah verses fixed to a doorpost.
Tzitzit: knotted threads the Torah requires on the corners of a four-cornered garment.
The blessing over wine that proclaims the holiness of Shabbat or a festival.

shabbat-26a-1-1.note: A mother-in-law who hated her daughter-in-law told her to go and adorn herself with balsam oil. She did. When she came back, the mother-in-law told her to go and light the lamp. She went and lit it, and she caught fire and was burned.
shabbat-26a-1-1.why: The Gemara is discussing why balsam sap may not be used to light the Shabbat lamp, and Abaye has given the reason that it is volatile and dangerous; the story shows how deadly that volatility can be.

terms.meaning: A fragrant oil made from the sap of the balsam tree, prized as a perfume. The Gemara treats it as highly flammable, so a woman anointed with it was in danger near an open flame.

shabbat-29b-5-5.note: Rabbi Yehuda recalled a Shabbat he spent in the upper room of the house of Nit'za in Lod. They were brought an eggshell, filled it with oil, pierced it and set it over the lamp so it would keep feeding the flame. Rabbi Tarfon and other Elders were there and said nothing to them. The Rabbis answered him that this proves nothing: the people of the house of Nit'za were vigilant.
shabbat-29b-5-5.why: The mishna records a dispute: the Rabbis forbid setting a pierced, oil-filled eggshell over a lamp on Shabbat, in case one takes oil from it; Rabbi Yehuda permits it and offers this Shabbat as proof. Afterward a Sage warns that the Elders' silence led to a mistaken leniency.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who permits the eggshell device and recalls using it in the house of Nit'za.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: One of the Elders present that Shabbat, who said nothing about the eggshell.

terms.meaning: The majority of Sages in a dispute, as opposed to the individual Sage who disagrees with them.
A room on the roof of a house, often used by the Sages for study and gatherings.
Senior Sages.

shabbat-30b-7-7.note: A man came before Rabbi and told him, "Your wife is my wife and your children are my children." Rabbi asked whether he would like a cup of wine; the man drank and burst. Another man came before Rabbi Hiyya and said, "Your mother is my wife and you are my son." Rabbi Hiyya offered him a cup of wine too, and he drank and burst. Rabbi Hiyya said Rabbi's prayer had protected him from having his children branded mamzerim, for after praying Rabbi used to ask God to save him that day from impudent people and from insolence.
shabbat-30b-7-7.why: The Gemara has just resolved two verses of Proverbs, one saying to answer a fool and one saying not to, by ruling that a fool is not answered on worldly matters; these two Sages, insulted personally, gave their accusers no reply.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, called simply Rabbi; a man claimed his wife and children as his own.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A Sage whom a man claimed as his son; he explains how Rabbi's prayer protected him.

terms.meaning: Children born of a forbidden union, such as adultery. In Jewish law they are barred from marrying most other Jews, so the charge was a grave slander on Rabbi's children.

shabbat-30b-8-8.note: Rabban Gamliel was teaching that in the future a woman will give birth every day, citing the verse "The woman with child and her that gives birth together." A student scoffed, quoting "There is nothing new under the sun." Rabban Gamliel said, "Come and I will show you an example of this in this world," took him outside, and showed him a hen.
shabbat-30b-8-8.why: The Gemara has resolved two verses of Proverbs by ruling that a fool is answered when he challenges the Torah, though not on worldly matters; Rabban Gamliel answering the scoffing student is its example of the first kind, followed by two more like it.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: A Sage teaching about the world to come who answered a scoffing student with a hen.

terms.meaning: Drew a teaching from a verse by reading it closely and creatively, beyond its plain sense.
The perfected world of the future that the Sages describe, in contrast to this world.

shabbat-30b-9-9.note: Rabban Gamliel taught that in the future trees will bear fruit every day, reading the verse "And it shall bring forth branches and bear fruit" to mean that just as a branch grows every day, so will fruit. The same student scoffed, "Isn't it written, there is nothing new under the sun?" Rabban Gamliel said he would show him an example in this world, went outside, and showed him a caper bush.
shabbat-30b-9-9.why: This is the second of three cases the Gemara gives for its ruling that a fool who challenges the Torah should be answered; it follows Rabban Gamliel's reply with the hen.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: A Sage teaching about the world to come who answered a scoffing student with a caper bush.

terms.meaning: A shrub with edible buds and fruit; some part of it can be eaten in every season, so it seems to bear produce all year.
The perfected world of the future that the Sages describe, in contrast to this world.

shabbat-30b-10-10.note: Rabban Gamliel taught that in the future the Land of Israel will bring forth ready-made cakes and fine woolen garments, citing "Let abundant grain be in the land." Once again the student scoffed that there is nothing new under the sun. Rabban Gamliel went outside and showed him truffles and mushrooms for the cakes, and for the woolen garments, the fibrous covering of a young palm branch.
shabbat-30b-10-10.why: This is the third of the cases the Gemara gives for its ruling that a fool who challenges the Torah should be answered; the Gemara then turns to Hillel's patience under provocation.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: A Sage teaching about the world to come who answered a scoffing student with mushrooms and palm fiber.

terms.meaning: Fungi that spring up from the ground overnight, here offered as a small-scale example of bread-like food growing from the earth.
The tender new growth at the top of a palm tree, wrapped in a thin, net-like covering that looks like woven cloth.

shabbat-30b-11-11.note: Two men made a bet: whoever could provoke Hillel into anger would win four hundred zuz. One of them chose Shabbat eve, while Hillel was washing his hair, and stood at his door calling rudely, Who here is Hillel? Each time Hillel wrapped himself, came out, called him my son, and patiently answered his insulting questions: why Babylonians have oval heads, why the people of Tadmor have bleary eyes, why Africans have wide feet. Finally the man burst out that he hoped there would not be many like Hillel in Israel, since he had lost four hundred zuz because of him. Hillel told him to watch his temper: Hillel is worth his losing four hundred zuz and four hundred more, and Hillel will not get upset.
shabbat-30b-11-11.why: The Gemara has just told how Rabban Gamliel calmly answered a scoffing student, and moves on to the patience of Sages. It quotes a teaching that one should always be patient like Hillel and not impatient like Shammai; this bet is its first example.

people.name: Hillel
people.about: A leading Sage, called the Nasi of Israel; a Babylonian, which the man's first question mocks.

people.name: Shammai
people.about: Named in the opening teaching as the example of an impatient man, set against Hillel.

terms.meaning: A silver coin. Four hundred zuz was a very large stake.
The title of the head of the Jewish community and its Sages in the Land of Israel.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law; the Gemara often quotes one with the words The Sages taught.

shabbat-31a-4-4.note: A non-Jew asked Shammai how many Torahs the Jews have. Shammai said two, the Written Torah and the Oral Torah. The man said he believed in the written one but not the oral one, and asked to be converted on condition that he would be taught only the Written Torah. Shammai scolded him and threw him out. He went to Hillel, who converted him. On the first day Hillel taught him the alphabet, alef, bet, gimmel, dalet; the next day he taught it in reverse. When the convert objected that this was not what he had been told yesterday, Hillel answered: you relied on me for that, so rely on me for the Oral Torah too.
shabbat-31a-4-4.why: It follows the story of the man who tried to make Hillel angry, in a run of episodes setting Hillel's patience against Shammai's impatience; this is the first of three about non-Jews who came to convert.

people.name: Shammai
people.about: A Sage who scolds the would-be convert and throws him out.

people.name: Hillel
people.about: A Sage who converts the man and then teaches him why he must trust oral teaching.

terms.meaning: The Written Torah is the text of the Five Books of Moses. The Oral Torah is the body of explanation and law passed down by teachers, which the Sages held was given alongside it.
The first four letters of the Hebrew alphabet.

shabbat-31a-5-5.note: A non-Jew came to Shammai and asked to be converted on condition that Shammai teach him the entire Torah while he stood on one foot. Shammai pushed him away with the builder's measuring stick in his hand. The man then came to Hillel, who converted him and told him: what is hateful to you, do not do to another. That is the entire Torah, and the rest is its interpretation. Go and study.
shabbat-31a-5-5.why: This is the second of three stories about non-Jews who asked Shammai and then Hillel to convert them; together they illustrate the teaching that one should be patient like Hillel and not impatient like Shammai.

people.name: Shammai
people.about: A Sage, said here to be a builder by trade, who pushes the man away with his measuring stick.

people.name: Hillel
people.about: A Sage who converts the man and sums up the Torah for him.

terms.meaning: A measuring stick a cubit long (roughly half a meter), used by builders.

shabbat-31a-6-8.note: A non-Jew overheard a teacher reading the list of the High Priest's garments and decided to convert so that he would be made High Priest. Shammai pushed him away; Hillel converted him and told him that only one who knows the royal protocols is made king, so go and learn them. Reading the Torah, the convert reached the verse that an outsider who comes near shall be put to death, and Hillel told him it applies even to King David. The convert reasoned that if it applies to Israel, whom God calls His firstborn, all the more to a convert who came with just his staff and bag. He blessed Hillel; later all three converts met and said Shammai's impatience sought to drive them from the world, while Hillel's patience brought them under the wings of the Divine Presence.
shabbat-31a-6-8.why: This third conversion story closes the run that began with the teaching to be patient like Hillel and not impatient like Shammai; the converts' own words at the end state that lesson. The Gemara then turns to other teachings about the conduct of the Sages.

people.name: Shammai
people.about: A Sage who pushes the would-be convert away.

people.name: Hillel
people.about: A Sage who converts the man and guides him to see why he cannot be High Priest; the convert calls him Hillel the patient.

people.name: David
people.about: King of Israel; Hillel says even he would be put to death for this.

terms.meaning: The chief priest who served in the Temple in Jerusalem; only a descendant of Aaron could hold the role.
An argument from the lesser to the greater: if a rule applies in the milder case, it applies all the more in the stronger one.

terms.term: under the wings of the Divine Presence
terms.meaning: A phrase for becoming part of the Jewish people and coming close to God, used especially of converts.

shabbat-33a-11-11.note: Shmuel HaKatan fell ill with hidrokan, a swelling disease, and prayed: Master of the Universe, who can tell why this has come? He was cured. Abaye also fell ill with it, and Rava said of him: I know that Nahmani starves himself. Rava himself then fell ill with it. The Gemara asks how, since Rava was the one who said that more people are killed by the chamber pot than by starvation, and answers that the Sages forced Rava to stay in place against his will while he taught.
shabbat-33a-11-11.why: The Gemara has just taught that there are three kinds of hidrokan: from sin, from hunger and from witchcraft. These three cases show Sages who fell ill with it for causes other than sin.

people.name: Shmuel HaKatan
people.about: A Sage who fell ill with hidrokan, prayed, and was cured.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage, called Nahmani here, who fell ill with hidrokan; Rava says he starves himself.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who vouches for Abaye and later falls ill with hidrokan himself.

terms.meaning: Edema, a disease in which the body swells with fluid. The Gemara says it can be a sign of sin, or come from hunger or witchcraft.
Rava's saying means that more people die from holding in their bodily needs than from hunger.

shabbat-33b-4-9.note: Rabbi Yehuda praised the Romans for their markets, bridges and bathhouses; Rabbi Yosei was silent; Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai said they built them only for themselves. Yehuda, son of converts, repeated this, and the government decreed that Yehuda be elevated, Yosei exiled, and Shimon killed. Shimon and his son hid in a cave for twelve years, fed by a miraculous carob tree and spring, until Elijah announced the emperor was dead. When they came out, everything they looked at burned, and a Divine Voice sent them back for twelve months. Later Shimon cleared a doubtfully impure marketplace for priests. An old man mocked him for purifying a cemetery; Shimon looked at him and he died, then turned Yehuda, son of converts, into a pile of bones.
shabbat-33b-4-9.why: A teaching just quoted calls Rabbi Yehuda the head of the speakers in every place. The Gemara asks how he got that title, and this story answers: the Roman government gave it to him after he praised them.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai
people.about: A Sage sentenced to death for criticizing the Romans; he hides in a cave with his son for over twelve years.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: Rabbi Shimon's son, who hides in the cave with him.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who praised the Romans and was elevated by them as the head of the speakers in every place.

people.name: Yehuda, son of converts
people.about: He repeated the Sages' words until the government heard them.

people.name: Rabbi Pinehas ben Ya'ir
people.about: Rabbi Shimon's son-in-law, who weeps at the cracks in his skin after the cave.

terms.meaning: The biblical prophet, who in Talmudic stories appears to Sages as a messenger.
A voice from heaven that announces God's will.
A religious status, not physical dirt; contact with a dead body passes it on, and priests had to avoid it, so a place where a body might be buried was off-limits to them.
A portion of produce given to priests, which may only be grown, handled and eaten in a state of ritual purity.

shabbat-39a-5-5.note: The people of Tiberias ran a pipe of cold water through a channel of hot water from the town's hot springs, so the water would be warm on Shabbat. The Sages prohibited them from using it.
shabbat-39a-5-5.why: The Gemara is weighing two reasons why insulating food in sun-heated sand is forbidden: a decree in case people use hot ashes, or the digging involved. The Tiberias case fits the first reason but not the second, so it is raised as an objection.

terms.meaning: The Sabbath, the weekly day of rest, on which cooking and heating food are forbidden.

shabbat-40a-7-7.note: At the bathhouse of Benei Berak the openings were sealed on the eve of a Festival to keep the heat in. The next day, on the Festival, Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya and Rabbi Akiva went in, sweated there, then came out and rinsed in the outer room. The hot water there was covered with boards. When the matter came before the Sages, they said this was allowed even where the hot water is not covered. Later, when the number of transgressors grew, they began to prohibit it. But one may walk through the large city bathhouses without concern.
shabbat-40a-7-7.why: A teaching has just ruled that on a Festival one may sweat in a bathhouse sealed the day before; Rabbi Yehuda brings this incident as an example, and the Gemara then explains who the transgressors were that led the Sages to forbid it.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: A Sage who sweated in the Benei Berak bathhouse on a Festival.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who sweated there with him.

terms.meaning: One of the biblical holy days, such as Passover or Sukkot, on which most work is forbidden, though some food preparation is allowed.
The cooler front room of a bathhouse, away from the hot water.

shabbat-40b-7-7.note: Rav Yitzhak bar Avdimi recalled following Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi into the bathhouse on Shabbat. He wanted to set a jar of oil in the hot bath to warm it for his teacher. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi told him instead to take water from the bath in a secondary vessel and put the oil in that.
shabbat-40b-7-7.why: The Sages are debating whether heating oil on Shabbat counts as cooking. The Gemara learns three rulings from this instruction: oil can be cooked, a secondary vessel does not cook, and even warming oil counts as cooking it.

people.name: Rav Yitzhak bar Avdimi
people.about: A student who tells the story of attending his teacher in the bathhouse.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, his teacher, who tells him how to warm the oil.

terms.meaning: A container that hot liquid has been poured into, rather than the one it was heated in. The Sages held it is not hot enough to cook.

shabbat-40b-9-9.note: A student of Rabbi Meir followed him into the bathhouse on Shabbat and wanted to rinse the floor. Rabbi Meir told him one may not rinse it. The student asked whether he could smear the floor with oil instead, and Rabbi Meir told him one may not smear it either.
shabbat-40b-9-9.why: The Gemara has asked how Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi could teach law inside a bathhouse, where Torah may not be discussed, and answered that stopping someone from breaking a law is different. Shmuel's report of Rabbi Meir doing the same is the proof.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A Sage who stops his student from rinsing or oiling the bathhouse floor on Shabbat.

shabbat-41a-4-5.note: Rabbi Zeira wanted to move from Babylonia to the Land of Israel, but his teacher Rav Yehuda held that leaving Babylonia for the Land of Israel violates a commandment, so Rabbi Zeira was avoiding him. Before leaving he decided to go and hear one more teaching from him. He found Rav Yehuda in the bathhouse telling his servant: bring me natron, bring me a comb, open your mouths and let out air, and drink from the bathhouse water. Rabbi Zeira said that had he come only to hear this, it would have been enough.
shabbat-41a-4-5.why: The Gemara has been discussing proper conduct while bathing. After the story it draws lessons from each of Rav Yehuda's instructions, such as that ordinary matters may be spoken in Hebrew in a bathhouse and why drinking hot water while bathing is healthy.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: Rav Yehuda's student, who wanted to emigrate to the Land of Israel against his teacher's view.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Rabbi Zeira's teacher, who held it was forbidden to leave Babylonia for the Land of Israel.

terms.meaning: The Land of Israel.
A natural mineral salt used as soap for washing.

shabbat-46a-7-7.note: Rav Avya came to Rava's house with clay on his feet and put them on the bed. Rava grew angry and set out to torment him with hard questions: why may a naphtha lamp be moved on Shabbat? Rav Avya said it can be used to cover a vessel. Rava objected that then every pebble in the yard could be moved too. Rav Avya answered that a lamp has the status of a vessel and pebbles do not, citing a baraita on jewelry and Ulla's reason for it. Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak said: Thank God that Rava did not embarrass Rav Avya.
shabbat-46a-7-7.why: Rabba and Rav Yosef have just ruled, against Rav Yehuda, that even a naphtha lamp may be moved on Shabbat; Rava's challenge asks for their reason, and Rav Avya supplies it.

people.name: Rav Avya
people.about: A guest at Rava's house who answers his hard questions

people.name: Rava
people.about: The host, angry at the dirtied bed

people.name: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak
people.about: The Sage who gives thanks that Rav Avya was not shamed

people.name: Ulla
people.about: A Sage whose reason Rav Avya cites

terms.meaning: A lamp burning crude oil, whose bad smell means it is used only for light.
Muktze: objects that may not be moved on Shabbat because they were not meant for use that day.
Being a usable utensil, which allows an object to be moved on Shabbat more freely than raw materials like pebbles.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

shabbat-48a-1-2.note: Rabba and Rabbi Zeira visited the house of the Exilarch on Shabbat and saw a servant set a jug of cold water on the mouth of a kettle of hot water. Rabba rebuked him. Rabbi Zeira asked how this differed from setting one urn on another, which is allowed; Rabba said that urn on urn only keeps heat in, while this creates new heat. Then the servant spread a kerchief over a vat and set a cup on it, and Rabba rebuked him again. When Rabbi Zeira asked why, Rabba said: wait and see. In the end the servant wrung out the kerchief. Rabba explained that a man cares about a kerchief and will wring it, unlike an ordinary cloth.
shabbat-48a-1-2.why: The Gemara has just distinguished food that is only kept warm from food that is actively heated, as when placed on olive residue. Rabba's first rebuke applies the same line: keeping heat in is allowed, creating heat is not.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: A Sage who twice rebukes the Exilarch's servant.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A Sage visiting with Rabba, who asks him to explain each rebuke.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia.
Wringing water out of cloth is one of the kinds of work forbidden on Shabbat.

shabbat-50b-8-8.note: Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi were sitting together on Shabbat when berada, a washing mixture, was brought to them. Ameimar and Rav Ashi washed with it; Mar Zutra did not. They asked him whether he did not accept Rav Sheshet's ruling that berada is permitted. Rav Mordekhai, who was there, told them not to learn from Mar Zutra, because he does not use it even on a weekday.
shabbat-50b-8-8.why: The Gemara has just defined berada and is discussing what may be used to wash on Shabbat. It then explains the split: Mar Zutra follows a teaching that forbids washing just to look good, while the others follow one telling a person to wash every day for the sake of his Maker.

people.name: Ameimar
people.about: A Sage who washes with berada on Shabbat.

people.name: Mar Zutra
people.about: A Sage who declines to wash with it.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage who washes with berada on Shabbat.

people.name: Rav Mordekhai
people.about: Present at the scene; he explains that Mar Zutra never uses berada, even on weekdays.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: A Sage whose ruling that berada is permitted the others cite.

terms.meaning: A washing powder that the Gemara says is a mixture of aloe, myrtle and violets.

shabbat-51b-10-10.note: Levi sent money to Bei Hozai to buy himself a Libyan donkey. The people there tied up his money and sent it back to him along with barley, as if to say that a donkey's stride depends on the barley it eats.
shabbat-51b-10-10.why: The Mishna has just mentioned a Libyan donkey with an iron halter, and Rav Huna has explained the term; having mentioned the Libyan donkey, the Gemara tells this anecdote about one.

people.name: Levi
people.about: A Sage who wanted to buy a Libyan donkey.

terms.meaning: A breed of donkey prized for its quality.
A region, which the story suggests was known for its donkeys.

shabbat-51b-17-17.note: Levi, son of Rav Huna bar Hiyya, and Rabba bar Rav Huna were travelling together when Levi's donkey went ahead of Rabba's. Rabba bar Rav Huna was offended. To make him feel better, Levi asked him a question of law: may a badly behaved donkey like this one go out on Shabbat with a halter? Rabba answered: your father said in the name of Shmuel that the law follows Hananya.
shabbat-51b-17-17.why: The Gemara has just concluded, through Rav Huna bar Hiyya in Shmuel's name, that the law follows Hananya: extra restraint on an animal is not a forbidden burden on Shabbat. In this story Rabba gives that ruling to Levi, son of the man who reported it.

people.name: Levi, son of Rav Huna bar Hiyya
people.about: A Sage whose donkey runs ahead; he asks a question to placate his companion.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage who is offended when Levi's donkey goes first, then answers his question.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage in whose name the ruling is given.

people.name: Hananya
people.about: An earlier Sage whose view, that extra restraint is not a burden, is the law.

terms.meaning: A harness of straps around an animal's head; a bit is usually enough for a donkey, so a halter is extra restraint.
On Shabbat an animal may not be made to carry a load into a public area. Gear that is not needed to control it may count as a load.

shabbat-53b-15-18.note: A man's wife died and left him a nursing baby, and he could not afford to pay a wet-nurse. A miracle happened: he grew breasts like a woman's and nursed his son himself. Rav Yosef said this showed how great the man was, that such a miracle was done for him; Abaye answered that, on the contrary, it showed how lowly he was, that the order of creation had to be changed for him. Rav Yehuda drew a different lesson: feeding a person is so hard that nature itself was altered, and Rav Naḥman added that miracles do happen, but food has never been created by one.
shabbat-53b-15-18.why: The Gemara has been discussing whether goats may go out on Shabbat with pouches on their udders, and has just told of goats in Antioch with huge udders; it attaches this related baraita about a miracle of nursing.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Sage who sees the miracle as proof of the man's greatness

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Answers Rav Yosef that the miracle shows the man's lowliness

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Sage who learns from the miracle how hard it is to provide a person's food

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: Sage who notes that miracles happen but food is never miraculously created

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core law code the Talmud discusses.
The natural order of the world as God made it; a miracle that changes it is seen here as unusual and even undignified.

shabbat-53b-19-19.note: A man married a woman who had only one arm, and he did not realize it until the day she died. Rav said: see how modest this woman was, that her husband never noticed. Rabbi Hiyya answered that this is to be expected of her, since a woman covers herself; rather, see how modest the man was, that he never noticed this about his wife.
shabbat-53b-19-19.why: The Gemara has just told the unusual story of a father who miraculously nursed his son, with the Sages arguing over what it says about him; it adds another unusual story over which two Sages differ in the same way.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage who praises the wife's modesty.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A Sage who says the praise belongs to the husband instead.

shabbat-55a-1-1.note: Rav Yehuda was sitting before his teacher Shmuel when a woman came and cried out before Shmuel, and he paid no attention to her. Rav Yehuda asked him whether he did not hold by the verse that whoever stops his ears at the cry of the poor will himself cry out and not be answered. Shmuel answered: Big-toothed one, your superior will be in cold water, but the superior of your superior will be in hot water. Mar Ukva sits here as president of the court.
shabbat-55a-1-1.why: The Gemara has just taught that anyone able to protest wrongdoing who does not is held responsible for it, and that leaders are judged most severely. Shmuel's answer puts the duty on Mar Ukva as head of the court; the Gemara then traces that duty to the house of David.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Shmuel's student, who challenges him for ignoring the woman.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Rav Yehuda's teacher, who ignores the woman's cry.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: The president of the court, who Shmuel says is responsible for such cases.

terms.meaning: Shmuel's image for punishment: the higher a person's authority, the harsher he is judged for failing to act.

shabbat-59b-7-7.note: People told Rav that a great, tall man who limped had come to Neharde'a and taught that a kelila ornament is permitted on Shabbat. Rav said: a great, tall man who limps must be Levi. From that he concluded that Rabbi Afes had died and Rabbi Hanina now sat at the head of the academy, so Levi had no one left to sit with and had come here.
shabbat-59b-7-7.why: The Gemara is debating whether a woman may go out on Shabbat wearing a kelila; this story reports Levi teaching that it is permitted, and the Gemara then tells how many women in Neharde'a went out wearing it after he did.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage who works out from a description who the visitor is and why he came.

people.name: Levi
people.about: A great, tall Sage with a limp who taught in Neharde'a that the kelila is permitted.

people.name: Rabbi Afes
people.about: Head of the academy, who Rav concludes has died.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: Who Rav concludes now heads the academy in Rabbi Afes's place.

terms.meaning: A crown-like headband worn by women, sometimes made of or set with metal; the question is whether wearing it outdoors on Shabbat counts as carrying.

shabbat-60a-8-11.note: Three Sages give three accounts of one disaster. Shmuel says Jews fleeing a religious persecution hid in a cave and agreed that anyone could come in but no one could go out; when one man's sandal was found reversed, they thought someone had left and that the enemy was coming, and in the panic they pushed one another and killed more of their own than the enemy had. Rabbi Elai ben Elazar says they heard a sound above the cave, and Rami bar Yehezkel says they heard it behind a synagogue; each time the same deadly crush followed.
shabbat-60a-8-11.why: The Mishna forbids going out on Shabbat in a spiked sandal, and the Gemara asks why. These accounts explain the ban as a memorial to a disaster caused by such a sandal, and the Gemara goes on to ask why the ban applies only on Shabbat and Festivals.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Sage who explains the ban with the story of the reversed sandal in the cave

people.name: Rabbi Elai ben Elazar
people.about: Sage who tells the version in which the hiders heard a sound above the cave

people.name: Rami bar Yeḥezkel
people.about: Sage who places the panic in a synagogue

terms.meaning: Government decrees forbidding Jewish practice; those who fled them went into hiding.
A sandal studded with nails, whose sound and prints the hiders mistook for the enemy's.

shabbat-63b-1-1.note: A pregnant woman went into a neighbor's house to bake in the oven there. The household dog barked at her, and her fetus was displaced. The owner told her not to be afraid, since the dog's teeth and claws had been removed. She answered: Take your kindness and throw it on the thorns; the fetus has already been displaced.
shabbat-63b-1-1.why: Reish Lakish has just taught that anyone who keeps a vicious dog keeps kindness out of his home, and Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak adds that he casts off the fear of Heaven. This incident shows the harm even a toothless dog can do.

terms.meaning: The fright caused her to lose the pregnancy; the Gemara's comment adds that the fetus will certainly die.

shabbat-63b-12-12.note: Rabba bar bar Hana, quoting Rabbi Yohanan, tells of a family in Jerusalem whose daughters walked with long strides, and as a result their hymens tore. The family made ankle bands for them and hung a chain between them so their steps would be short, and the hymens no longer tore. Rabbi Yirmeya was woken by the sound of the chains and said: Correct, and Rabbi Yohanan said the same.
shabbat-63b-12-12.why: The Gemara is asking why a chain makes a garter count as a vessel that can become ritually impure, when the chain seems to do nothing. This account is the answer: the chain performs a real function, keeping a girl's stride short.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Ḥana
people.about: Sage who reports the account in Rabbi Yohanan's name

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Sage in whose name the account is told

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya
people.about: Sage woken by the voices or chains who approves the practice

terms.meaning: Only objects that count as functioning vessels can contract ritual impurity; the question is whether the chain gives the garter that status.

shabbat-65a-14-14.note: Shmuel's father did not let his daughters go out with strings in their ears, did not let them sleep next to each other, and made ritual baths for them in the spring month of Nisan, and in the autumn month of Tishrei laid mats on the bed of the Euphrates so they could immerse without sinking into the mud.
shabbat-65a-14-14.why: The Mishna has just permitted young girls to go out on Shabbat with strings in their pierced ears. The Gemara cites this father's stricter practice and then examines each of his customs in turn, starting with how he could forbid what the Mishna allows.

people.name: Shmuel’s father
people.about: Father of the Sage Shmuel, who set strict rules for his daughters

terms.meaning: A pool of water (mikveh) in which a person immerses to become ritually pure.
Hebrew months: Nisan falls in spring, after the rainy season; Tishrei falls in early autumn, after the dry summer.

shabbat-65b-2-2.note: Shmuel's father made a ritual bath for his daughters during the spring month of Nisan rather than letting them immerse in the Euphrates. The Gemara explains he held that the river was then swollen with rain, and that water which had fallen as rain might outweigh the river's own flowing water, so immersing there would not purify them.
shabbat-65b-2-2.why: The Gemara is working through the customs of Shmuel's father one by one. This one is said to support Rav's view that the Euphrates swells from rain in the Land of Israel, and to disagree with Shmuel's view that the river is fed from its own bed.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Sage who said the Euphrates is the great witness to rain falling in the Land of Israel

terms.meaning: The Land of Israel, as seen from Babylonia.
Spring or river water purifies even while it flows; rainwater purifies only when gathered in a pool, not while flowing.

shabbat-67b-14-14.note: Rabbi Akiva held a banquet for his son. Over every cup of wine he brought, he said: Wine and life to the mouth of the Sages; life and wine to the mouth of the Sages and to the mouth of their students.
shabbat-67b-14-14.why: The discussion is listing practices that are or are not forbidden as superstitious 'ways of the Amorite'. The toast 'wine and life to the mouth of the Sages' is ruled permitted, and Rabbi Akiva's banquet shows a great Sage using it.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Sage who made a banquet for his son and toasted the Sages over each cup

terms.meaning: Superstitious or pagan practices the Torah forbids imitating.

shabbat-74a-5-5.note: Rav Dimi, arriving from the Land of Israel, reported that it was Rav Beivai's Shabbat to host the students, and Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi happened to come. Rav Beivai set before them a basket of fruit without sorting out the leaves and stems. Rav Dimi said he did not know whether Rav Beivai did this because he held that picking food out of waste is forbidden on Shabbat, or because he wanted to show generosity with a full basket.
shabbat-74a-5-5.why: The Gemara is debating how far the Shabbat ban on sorting reaches, including whether taking food out of waste is forbidden. Rav Dimi's report might have settled it, but he himself says it proves nothing, since there are two possible reasons for what Rav Beivai did.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: Sage who came from the Land of Israel and reported the incident

people.name: Rav Beivai
people.about: Sage whose turn it was to host, who served unsorted fruit

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Sage who visited Rav Beivai on that Shabbat

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: Sage who visited Rav Beivai with Rabbi Ami

terms.meaning: One of the labors forbidden on Shabbat: sorting wanted from unwanted items, such as food from waste.

shabbat-80b-2-2.note: Rav Beivai smeared his daughter with lime limb by limb, a little at a time, to remove her hair, and when he married her off he received four hundred zuz for her. A gentile neighbor with a daughter smeared her whole body with lime at once, and she died. He said: Rav Beivai killed my daughter. Rav Nahman commented that Rav Beivai's family drinks beer, so their daughters need lime treatment; we who do not drink beer have daughters who do not need it.
shabbat-80b-2-2.why: The Mishna sets the amount of lime one is liable for carrying on Shabbat by its use as a depilatory on girls, and Rav has explained that use. The story about Rav Beivai's daughter follows on that use of lime.

people.name: Rav Beivai
people.about: Sage who treated his daughter with lime gradually before her marriage

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: Sage who links the need for lime to drinking beer

terms.meaning: A silver coin; four hundred zuz was a large sum.
A caustic mineral paste spread on the skin to remove hair.

shabbat-81a-4-4.note: A man named Zunin came into the study hall and asked the Sages what size the stones a person may carry into the bathroom on Shabbat for wiping must be. They answered: the size of an olive, a nut, or an egg. He asked them: Should he take scales into the bathroom? The Sages took a vote and concluded that he may simply take a handful.
shabbat-81a-4-4.why: The Mishna has been setting minimum sizes of stones for liability on Shabbat. The story turns to how big bathroom stones moved on Shabbat must be, and a baraita (a teaching from the Mishna's era left out of the Mishna) records the same two views, from Rabbi Yosei and his son.

people.name: Zunin
people.about: Man who came into the study hall and challenged the Sages' measures

terms.meaning: Standard units of volume used in Jewish law, based on the size of an olive, a nut and an egg.

shabbat-81b-5-5.note: Rav Hisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna were traveling by boat when a certain noblewoman asked to sit with them, and they refused. She said a spell and stopped the boat; they said something of their own and freed it. She said to them: What can I do to you, since you do not wipe yourselves with an earthenware shard, do not kill lice on your clothes, and do not pull a vegetable out of a gardener's bundle and eat it before untying it?
shabbat-81b-5-5.why: Rabbi Yohanan forbade wiping with an earthenware shard, and the Gemara considered whether the reason is witchcraft. When it asks what witchcraft has to do with it, this story answers: the woman names wiping with a shard as one of the openings witchcraft uses.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Sage traveling on the boat who refused the woman a seat

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Huna
people.about: Sage traveling with Rav Hisda

terms.meaning: A Roman noblewoman; here one who practices witchcraft.

shabbat-88a-8-8.note: A heretic watched Rava so absorbed in study that he did not notice he was squeezing his fingers under his leg until they spurted blood. The heretic said: You impulsive nation, who put your mouths before your ears; you are still impulsive. You should have listened first and accepted the commands only if you could keep them. Rava answered with a verse: of us, who walk wholeheartedly, it is written, 'The integrity of the upright will guide them,' while of those who walk in deceit it says, 'The perverseness of the faithless will destroy them.'
shabbat-88a-8-8.why: The Sages have just praised Israel for saying 'We will do' before 'We will hear' at Sinai, a secret of the angels. The heretic mocks that very order as recklessness, and Rava defends it as wholehearted trust.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Sage so absorbed in study that he did not notice his fingers bleeding

terms.meaning: Someone who rejected the Sages' teachings and often argued with them.
Israel's promise at Sinai, 'We will do and we will hear', which put doing before hearing what was required.

shabbat-104a-3-3.note: The Sages told Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that young children had come to the study hall and said things not heard even in the days of Joshua bin Nun. Going through the Hebrew alphabet, they read the letters as lessons: alef-beit means 'learn wisdom', gimmel-dalet means 'give to the poor', and the gimmel's leg reaches toward the dalet because the generous run after the poor. They read the open and closed forms of letters as open and hidden teachings, and as humble righteous people who will one day be known, and the shapes of kuf and reish as God turning from the wicked while leaving an opening through which he can return.
shabbat-104a-3-3.why: The Gemara has been discussing the open and closed forms of letters such as mem and samekh and how old those forms are; the children's teaching gives a meaning to those letter shapes.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: The Sage to whom the report of the children's teaching is brought

terms.meaning: The house of study where Sages and students learned Torah together.
Several Hebrew letters (mem, nun, tzadi, peh, kaf) are written in one shape in the middle of a word and another at the end.
The life after this one, where the righteous are rewarded.

shabbat-108a-5-8.note: Shmuel and Karna, sitting by the Malka River, saw the water rising and murky. Shmuel said a great man with aching intestines was coming from the Land of Israel, and sent Karna to test him. Karna found Rav and quizzed him on why phylacteries are written only on kosher hide, why forbidden blood is red, and why circumcision is done where it is; Rav answered each from verses. Rav asked his name, and on hearing Karna, said: May a horn grow in his eyes. Shmuel then took Rav home, fed him barley bread, fried fish and beer, and did not show him the lavatory so he would have diarrhea. Rav cursed: Whoever causes me suffering, let his children not survive. And so it was.
shabbat-108a-5-8.why: The Gemara has just asked whether phylacteries may be written on fish skin. Karna's question about writing them only on the hide of a kosher animal, and Rav's answer from a verse, bear on that question, and the Gemara goes on to the same derivations in other teachings.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Sage who foresaw Rav's arrival, sent Karna to test him, and then hosted him

people.name: Karna
people.about: Sage sent by Shmuel to test Rav with questions

people.name: Rav
people.about: The great man arriving from the Land of Israel, who answered Karna and cursed his host

terms.meaning: Tefillin: leather boxes holding Torah passages, worn on the arm and head; the passages are written on parchment from an animal hide.
The Land of Israel, as seen from Babylonia.
An idiom for testing someone to see whether he is a real Torah scholar.

shabbat-109a-2-2.note: Rav Hisda said melon juice is permitted on Shabbat but the juice of pipuim is not. Ze'iri's wife made melon juice for Hiyya bar Ashi, and he would not eat it. She said to him: I made it for your teacher, and he ate it, and you will not? The Gemara explains that Ze'iri was following his own ruling that clear wine and water may be poured through a strainer on Shabbat, since that does nothing to them; so too melon juice, drunk the way it is, involves doing nothing.
shabbat-109a-2-2.why: The discussion is listing foods and drinks that may or may not be taken on Shabbat when they could count as medicine. The incident shows a student holding back from a drink his own teacher allowed himself.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Sage who permitted melon juice on Shabbat

people.name: Ze’iri
people.about: Sage, Hiyya bar Ashi's teacher, who ate the melon juice his wife made

people.name: Ḥiyya bar Ashi
people.about: Ze'iri's student, who refused the melon juice

terms.meaning: A kind of vegetable whose juice Rav Hisda forbade on Shabbat.
A cloth or sieve for straining dregs from wine; straining is restricted on Shabbat.

shabbat-109a-4-5.note: Ravina visited Rav Ashi and saw that a donkey had stepped on the back of Rav Ashi's foot, and Rav Ashi was sitting soaking it in vinegar on Shabbat. Ravina asked whether he did not hold with Rav Hillel that vinegar is not permitted. Rav Ashi answered that the back of the hand and the back of the foot are different. In another version Rav Ashi was soaking his foot in wine, and Ravina reminded him of Rava's view that even wine heals delicate people like him; Rav Ashi gave the same answer, citing Rav that such a wound is like a mortal wound, for which Shabbat may be violated.
shabbat-109a-4-5.why: Mar Ukva has just allowed soaking a wound in wine on Shabbat, while Rav Hillel ruled out vinegar and Rava ruled out wine for delicate people. The incident adds an exception: wounds on the back of the hand or foot are treated as dangerous.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Sage who visited Rav Ashi and questioned his treatment

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Sage whose foot was stepped on by a donkey

terms.meaning: The Sages forbade most medical treatment on Shabbat, except where life may be in danger, when Shabbat may be violated.
A Babylonian town whose people Rava called delicate.

shabbat-109b-8-8.note: Rav Ahadvoi bar Ami's mother treated a man who had drunk exposed water. She boiled one rose with one cup of beer and gave it to him to drink. Then she lit the oven, swept out the coals, set a brick inside, and sat him on it. Something like a green leaf came out of him.
shabbat-109b-8-8.why: The Gemara has just given a remedy for drinking water a snake may have poisoned: five roses cooked in five cups of beer. This woman's cure used one of each, and it worked.

people.name: Rav Aḥadvoi bar Ami’s mother
people.about: Woman who treated a man who had drunk exposed water

terms.meaning: Water left uncovered, which the Sages feared a snake had drunk from and left venom in.

shabbat-109b-10-10.note: Rav Shimi bar Ashi saw a man who had swallowed a snake. Appearing to him as a horseman, he fed him hops with salt and made him run ahead of him for three mil, and the snake came out of him in pieces; another version says Rav Shimi himself swallowed the snake and Elijah, appearing as a horseman, did this for him. In Pumbedita a Jewish official was bitten by a snake. All thirteen white donkeys in the town were torn open for the cure and found unfit, and a lion ate the last one before it could be brought. Abaye said he must have been bitten by a snake of the Rabbis, which has no cure; they confirmed he had defied Rav Yitzhak bar Bisna's ban on bringing myrtle and palm branches with bells to a wedding hall. He died.
shabbat-109b-10-10.why: The Gemara is listing folk remedies: hops in salt and a three-mil run for one who swallowed a snake, and a torn-open white donkey fetus for a snakebite, but only if it is not unfit. Each incident follows one of these remedies.

people.name: Rav Shimi bar Ashi
people.about: Sage who cured a man who swallowed a snake, or in another version was cured himself

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who in one version appeared as a horseman and cured Rav Shimi

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Sage who explained why the official's bite could not be cured

people.name: Rav Yitzḥak bar Bisna
people.about: Sage whose ban, made when Rav died, the official defied

terms.meaning: A distance of roughly a kilometer.
An animal with a defect that will kill it within twelve months; the remedy works only with a healthy one.
A bite sent as punishment for breaking a rule of the Sages, based on the verse 'one who breaches a fence will be bitten by a snake'.

shabbat-110b-4-4.note: A certain Arab sick with jaundice said to a gardener: Take my cloak and give me a row of leeks. The gardener gave him the row and he ate it. Then the Arab said: Lend me your cloak so I can sleep in it a little. He wrapped himself in it and slept, and when he grew hot and stood up, pieces fell from it bit by bit.
shabbat-110b-4-4.why: The Gemara is listing remedies for jaundice, ending with sharp leeks from the middle of a row. The story shows that last remedy at work, followed by the sweating cure in a wrap the discussion described earlier.

terms.meaning: An illness that turns the skin yellow; the Gemara lists many folk cures for it.

shabbat-112a-7-7.note: Rabbi Yirmeya was walking behind Rabbi Abbahu on Shabbat in a karmelit when his sandal strap tore. Rabbi Abbahu told him to wrap a moist reed, fit for animal fodder, around it. Another time Abaye was standing before Rav Yosef when his strap tore, and Rav Yosef told him to leave the sandal where it was. Abaye asked why his case differed from Rabbi Yirmeya's; Rav Yosef said that there the sandal would not have been safe, while here it would be. Abaye objected that the sandal was still usable, since he could switch it to the other foot, but Rav Yosef answered that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda, under whose view it no longer counts as a usable item.
shabbat-112a-7-7.why: The Gemara has been asking when tying sandal straps on Shabbat is forbidden or permitted. These two incidents turn to a torn strap: whether the sandal may be fixed or moved, which depends on whether it still counts as a utensil.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya
people.about: Sage whose sandal strap tore while walking behind Rabbi Abbahu

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: Sage who told Rabbi Yirmeya to wrap the sandal with a reed

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Sage whose strap tore while standing before Rav Yosef

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Abaye's teacher, who told him to leave the sandal

terms.meaning: An area such as a field or side street that is neither fully private nor fully public; the Sages restricted carrying there on Shabbat.
An object fit for use; on Shabbat one may move utensils but not broken objects that have lost that status.

shabbat-115a-6-6.note: Rabbi Yosei tells of his father, Ḥalafta, who visited Rabban Gamliel in Tiberias and found him at the table of Yoḥanan HaNazuf, reading an Aramaic translation of the book of Job. Yoḥanan told Rabban Gamliel he remembered his grandfather, also Rabban Gamliel, standing on a step on the Temple Mount when a translated Job was brought to him; he told the builder to bury it under a row of bricks. Hearing this, Rabban Gamliel ordered the book buried. Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda says a bowl of mortar was turned over on it, but Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi objects: where would mortar come from on the Temple Mount, and may one destroy such writings by hand? Rather, they are left in a neglected place to decay.
shabbat-115a-6-6.why: Rav Huna and Rav Ḥisda disagree whether holy books in translation may be rescued from a fire on Shabbat. Rav Huna says early Sages already disagreed, and Rabbi Yosei, who says they are not rescued, tells this incident.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Tells the incident about his father

people.name: Ḥalafta
people.about: Rabbi Yosei's father, who visited Rabban Gamliel

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Was reading a translation of Job and ordered it buried

people.name: Yoḥanan HaNazuf
people.about: Rabban Gamliel's host, who recalled what his grandfather did

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Rejects the detail about the bowl of mortar

terms.term: translation of the book of Job
terms.meaning: A rendering of the biblical book into Aramaic, the everyday language of many Jews at the time, rather than the original Hebrew.
The hill in Jerusalem on which the Temple stood.

shabbat-115b-1-1.note: A teaching of the Sages says that written blessings and amulets, even though they contain God's name and passages of Torah, are left to burn in a fire on Shabbat; so, the Sages said, those who write blessings are like those who burn the Torah. A man in Sidon was writing such blessings. Rabbi Yishmael was told and went to check. As Rabbi Yishmael climbed the ladder, the man sensed him coming and plunged his bundle of blessings into a basin of water. Rabbi Yishmael told him that the punishment for this second act was greater than for the first.
shabbat-115b-1-1.why: The Gemara is working out which sacred writings may be rescued from a fire on Shabbat, including scrolls in other languages; this teaching adds blessings and amulets to the texts that are not rescued.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: The Sage who goes to check on the man writing blessings and rebukes him.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of their rulings.
Written charms worn for protection, which could contain names of God and verses from the Torah.
Here, written-out texts of prayers and blessings; the Sages of that time opposed writing them down.

shabbat-116a-10-10.note: Imma Shalom, wife of Rabbi Eliezer and sister of Rabban Gamliel, lived near a Christian philosopher reputed not to take bribes. To mock and expose him, she secretly gave him a golden lamp, then came before him with her brother asking for a share of her father's estate. He ruled they should divide it. Rabban Gamliel said their Torah gives a daughter nothing where there is a son; the philosopher said the Torah of Moses had been replaced by a book where son and daughter inherit alike. Next day Rabban Gamliel gave him a Libyan donkey, and he ruled that the book had not come to change the Torah, so the daughter does not inherit. She said, 'May your light shine like a lamp'; Rabban Gamliel said, 'The donkey came and kicked the lamp.'
shabbat-116a-10-10.why: The Gemara has been discussing the books of heretics and whether they are saved from fire, and has just given Rabbi Yohanan's mocking name for the Christian Gospel, 'avon gilyon'; this story shows that name in use.

people.name: Imma Shalom
people.about: Wife of Rabbi Eliezer and sister of Rabban Gamliel; she gives the philosopher a golden lamp.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Imma Shalom's brother, who argues the case with her and gives the philosopher a donkey.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: Imma Shalom's husband; named only to identify her.

terms.meaning: A wordplay on the Greek 'Evangelion' (the Gospel), meaning roughly 'the sinful page'.
Here a Christian judge or scholar living in their neighborhood, known for claiming he took no bribes.

shabbat-118b-13-13.note: Rav Yosef asked Rav Yosef son of Rabba which mitzva his father had been most careful about. He answered: the ritual fringes. One day, climbing the stairs, his father had a string of his fringes snap, and he would not go down until a new string was put on. Then other Sages name deeds they hope to be rewarded for. Abaye makes a feast for the Sages when a young scholar finishes a tractate. Rava does not go to sleep before searching out every argument in favor of a young scholar who comes before him for judgment. Mar bar Rav Ashi disqualifies himself from judging a young scholar, because he loves him like himself, and no one sees his own faults.
shabbat-118b-13-13.why: The Gemara is collecting sayings in which Sages name the mitzva they kept best and hope to be rewarded for; Rav Naḥman has just boasted of his fringes, and Rabba's fringes and these further boasts continue the list.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Asks what Rabba was most careful about

people.name: Rav Yosef son of Rabba
people.about: Tells about his father's care with his fringes

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Hopes for reward for feasting the Sages when a young scholar finishes a tractate

people.name: Rava
people.about: Hopes for reward for seeking a young scholar's merits when judging him

people.name: Mar bar Rav Ashi
people.about: Refuses to judge a young scholar because he loves him like himself

terms.meaning: Strings the Torah commands to be tied to the corners of a four-cornered garment.
One volume of the Mishna or Talmud, devoted to one area of law.
A commandment of the Torah, or a good deed done in obedience to one.

shabbat-119a-4-4.note: A rich gentile lived near a man called Yosef who cherishes Shabbat. Astrologers told the gentile that Yosef would end up consuming all his property, so he sold everything, bought a pearl and put it in his hat. Crossing a river, the wind blew the hat into the water and a fish swallowed it. The fish was caught late on Friday afternoon, and the townspeople sent the fishermen to Yosef, who always bought fine food for Shabbat. He bought it, cut it open, found the pearl and sold it for thirteen vessels of gold coins. An old man who met him said: one who lends to Shabbat, Shabbat repays him.
shabbat-119a-4-4.why: The Gemara is collecting accounts of how Sages honored Shabbat by preparing for it themselves; this story shows the reward for spending on Shabbat, and leads into the question of what merit makes people wealthy.

people.name: Yosef who cherishes Shabbat
people.about: A Jew known for buying fine food in honor of Shabbat.

people.name: the gentile
people.about: Yosef's rich neighbor, who tries to escape the astrologers' prediction.

terms.meaning: The Sabbath, the weekly day of rest from Friday evening to Saturday night.
Here called Chaldeans: people who foretold the future from the stars.

shabbat-119a-6-6.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi asked Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, how the wealthy in lands without Sages earn their wealth. He answered: because they honor Shabbat, and cited Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba. Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba told of staying with a householder in Laodicea who was served at a gold table so heavy it took sixteen men to carry, hung with silver chains and set with dishes and every kind of food. When it was set down they recited 'The earth and all that fills it is God's,' and when it was taken away, 'The heavens are God's heavens, but the earth He gave to mankind.' Asked how he had earned this, the host said he had been a butcher who set aside the finest animal each time for Shabbat. Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba told him he was fortunate and blessed God for this merit.
shabbat-119a-6-6.why: This is the last of three answers: the wealthy of the Land of Israel earn it by tithing, those of Babylonia by honoring the Torah, and those elsewhere by honoring Shabbat, which this account is brought to prove.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: The Sage who asks how the wealthy of different lands earn their wealth.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage who answers that they honor Shabbat.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba
people.about: The Sage who stayed with the rich householder in Laodicea and tells the story.

terms.meaning: A city where Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba was a guest, outside the lands where the Sages lived.

shabbat-121a-4-4.note: A fire broke out on Shabbat in the courtyard of Yosef ben Simai in Shihin. Soldiers came from the fortress of Tzippori to put it out, because he was a steward of the king, but he would not let them, out of respect for Shabbat. A miracle happened: rain fell and put out the fire. That evening he sent two sela coins to each soldier and fifty to their commander. When the Sages heard, they said he need not have stopped them, citing the rule that one tells a gentile neither 'put it out' nor 'don't put it out.'
shabbat-121a-4-4.why: The mishna says a Jew need not tell a gentile to put out or leave a fire on Shabbat, and the Gemara has just argued over whether one may hint 'whoever puts it out will not lose'; this incident shows the Sages applying the mishna to a real fire.

people.name: Yosef ben Simai
people.about: A steward of the king whose courtyard caught fire on Shabbat and who refused the soldiers' help.

terms.meaning: A manager of the king's property or affairs.
A silver coin.
The core collection of the early Sages' rulings, which the Gemara discusses.

shabbat-121a-7-7.note: Rav Yehuda, Rav Yirmeya bar Abba and Rav Hanan bar Rava came to stay at the house of Avin of Nashikiya. Beds were brought for the first two but not for Rav Hanan bar Rava. He then found Avin teaching his son the mishna that allows covering a child's feces with a bowl on Shabbat. Rav Hanan said, 'Avin the fool is teaching his son folly,' arguing that the feces are food for dogs and may simply be moved. Avin asked how he should teach it instead, and Rav Hanan told him to say 'chicken feces.'
shabbat-121a-7-7.why: The mishna permits covering a child's feces with a bowl on Shabbat; Rav Hanan's challenge to that very line opens the Gemara's discussion, which goes on to ask why such feces could not just be removed.

people.name: Rav Hanan bar Rava
people.about: A guest who is not given a bed and then mocks his host's teaching.

people.name: Avin
people.about: The host, from Nashikiya, who is teaching his son the mishna.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: One of the guests, who is given a bed.

people.name: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba
people.about: One of the guests, who is given a bed.

terms.meaning: The core collection of the early Sages' rulings; here, the ruling that one may cover a child's feces with a bowl on Shabbat.
Limits on how far people and things may be moved on Shabbat; Rav Hanan cites flowing water, which has none, to argue the feces count as ready for use.

shabbat-121b-7-7.note: Rabbi Abba bar Kahana reported that once a snake fell into the study hall on Shabbat, and a Nabatean stood up and killed it. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said: 'One of its type killed it.'
shabbat-121b-7-7.why: The Gemara is debating whether snakes and scorpions may be killed on Shabbat; right after, it asks whether Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's remark meant the man had acted properly or not.

people.name: Rabbi Abba bar Kahana
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: The leading Sage, who remarks on the killing of the snake.

people.name: the Nabatean
people.about: A man of the Nabatean people who killed the snake.

terms.meaning: A member of a non-Jewish people of the region.

shabbat-121b-9-9.note: Abba bar Marta, also called Abba bar Manyomi, owed money to the household of the Exilarch, and they brought him there on Shabbat and tormented him to make him pay. Some spittle was on the floor, and the Exilarch told his household to bring a vessel and put it over the spittle. Abba bar Manyomi told them there was no need, since Rav Yehuda ruled that one may step on spittle in passing. The Exilarch said: he is a Torah scholar, leave him alone.
shabbat-121b-9-9.why: The Gemara has just cited Rav Yehuda's ruling that one may tread on spittle on Shabbat without intending to smooth the ground; this story shows the ruling being quoted in practice.

people.name: Abba bar Marta
people.about: Also called Abba bar Manyomi; a scholar who owed money to the Exilarch's household.

people.name: the Exilarch
people.about: Head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, whose household held Abba's debt.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia.

shabbat-122b-1-1.note: Shmuel came to the house of Avin Toran. A gentile came in and lit a lamp, and Shmuel turned his face away so as not to benefit from its light. When he saw the gentile bring a document and read it, Shmuel said the man had lit it for his own use, and turned his face back toward the lamp.
shabbat-122b-1-1.why: The Gemara is asking when a Jew may use a lamp a gentile lit on Shabbat, concluding that it depends on whom the gentile lit it for; Shmuel's behavior shows that test applied.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage visiting Avin Toran's house on Shabbat.

people.name: Avin Toran
people.about: The host whose house Shmuel visited.

shabbat-124b-20-20.note: Rava was walking along a street in Mehoza when his shoes got dirty with clay. His servant picked up a piece of broken pottery from the street and wiped them. The Sages there shouted at him. Rava said: is it not enough that they have not learned, they also teach others?
