If the shard were in a courtyard it could be used to cover a vessel; here too it is useful to me.
shabbat-124b-20-20.why: Rava has just ruled, against Shmuel and Rav Nahman, that a small pottery shard may be moved on Shabbat even in the public domain; this story shows him acting on that view.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage whose servant wipes his shoes with a shard on Shabbat.

people.name: Rava's servant
people.about: Wipes the clay off Rava's shoes with a shard from the street.

terms.meaning: A broken piece of an earthenware pot.
In Shabbat law, a street or open area used by the public, as opposed to a private courtyard.

shabbat-125b-6-7.note: Rav Dimi reported in Rabbi Hanina's name that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi once came to a place and found a row of building stones. He told his students to go and have in mind to sit on them the next day, Shabbat, without doing anything to the stones. Rabbi Yohanan disagreed: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi did require an action. Rabbi Ami said he told them to arrange the stones; Rabbi Asi said he told them to rub off the mortar.
shabbat-125b-6-7.why: Rabba and Rav Yosef disagree whether an object set aside from use on Shabbat needs an action, or only a thought, to make it usable; the Gemara shows Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi holding the same split views in their versions of this incident.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: The leading Sage, who tells his students to prepare the stones for sitting on Shabbat.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Says Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi required an action, not just a thought.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Says the instruction was to arrange the stones.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: Says the instruction was to rub the mortar off them.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: Brought the report from the Land of Israel to Babylonia.

terms.meaning: Things not meant for use on Shabbat, which therefore may not be moved then unless prepared beforehand.

shabbat-127a-8-9.note: Rabba reported that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi once came to a place too crowded for his students, went out to a field full of sheaves of grain and cleared the whole field. Rav Yosef reported the same incident about Rabbi Hiyya: he too found the place too crowded, went out to a field of sheaves and cleared all of it.
shabbat-127a-8-9.why: The mishna lets one move four or five baskets of produce on Shabbat to make room for guests, and the Gemara asks whether more is allowed for more guests; these reports prove it depends on the number of guests.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: The leading Sage who, in one version, clears a field to make room for students.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: The Sage who, in the other version, clears the field.

terms.meaning: Bundles of cut grain stalks.

shabbat-127b-1-4.note: A man from the Upper Galilee worked three years for a householder in the south. On the eve of Yom Kippur he asked for his wages to feed his family. To every request, for money, produce, land, animals or bedding, the householder said 'I have none,' and the worker went home in anguish. After Sukkot the householder brought the wages and three donkeys loaded with food, drink and sweets. After they ate, he asked what the worker had suspected; for each refusal the worker had imagined an innocent reason, ending with 'perhaps he consecrated all his property to Heaven.' The householder swore it was so: he had vowed away his property because his son Hyrcanus would not study Torah, and the Sages had released his vows. He said: as you judged me favorably, so may God judge you favorably.
shabbat-127b-1-4.why: Rabbi Yohanan has just listed judging others favorably among the deeds whose reward is enjoyed in this world as well as the next; this teaching, that one who judges others favorably is judged favorably, is illustrated by the worker.

people.name: the worker
people.about: A man from the Upper Galilee who worked three years without pay and judged his employer favorably.

people.name: the householder
people.about: The employer who said he had nothing, then came to pay with gifts.

people.name: Hyrcanus
people.about: The householder's son, who did not study Torah.

terms.meaning: The Day of Atonement, the holiest fast day of the Jewish year.
Given to the Temple; property dedicated this way could not be used or paid out to anyone.
The Sages had the power to annul a vow that a person regretted.
Produce from which the required portions for priests, Levites and the poor had been taken; untithed produce may not be eaten or given.

shabbat-127b-5-7.note: A pious man redeemed a young Jewish woman from captivity. At the inn he had her sleep at his feet. The next morning he went down, immersed in a ritual bath, and taught his students. He asked what they had suspected when she lay at his feet; they said perhaps one of the students was not trusted and he wanted to protect her. He asked what they had suspected when he immersed; they said perhaps the strain of the journey had caused him a seminal emission. He swore by the Temple service that this was so, and said: as you judged me favorably, so may God judge you favorably.
shabbat-127b-5-7.why: This is the second in a run of teachings about judging others favorably, following the worker who imagined innocent reasons for his employer's refusals; here students do the same for their teacher.

people.name: the pious man
people.about: A man who redeemed a captive woman and later asked his students what they had suspected of him.

terms.meaning: A pool of water used for immersion to become ritually pure.
A discharge of semen, which made a man ritually impure until he immersed.
An oath formula, swearing by the worship once done in the Temple in Jerusalem.

shabbat-127b-8-12.note: The Torah scholars needed something from a Roman matron whom all the great men of Rome visited, and asked who would go. Rabbi Yehoshua said he would. With his students, he took off his phylacteries four cubits from her door, went in and locked the door behind him. When he came out he immersed in a ritual bath and taught his students. He asked what they had suspected at each step; they answered that holy objects may not enter an impure place, that perhaps there was a royal matter between them, and that perhaps some of her spittle had sprayed onto his clothes. He swore by the Temple service that this was so, and said: as you judged me favorably, so may God judge you favorably.
shabbat-127b-8-12.why: This is the third teaching in a row about students judging a teacher favorably when his conduct looked suspicious; the Gemara then returns to the mishna's list of what may be moved on Shabbat.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: The Sage who goes to the matron and then asks his students what they suspected of him.

terms.meaning: A noble Roman woman, here one with influence among the great men of Rome.
Small leather boxes holding Torah passages, worn on the arm and head; in Hebrew, tefillin.
About two meters; a cubit is a forearm's length.
The Sages ruled that a gentile's spittle is ritually impure, which is why he would immerse if it touched his clothes.

shabbat-129a-8-8.note: Rav Hisda's daughter, Rava's wife, immersed in a ritual bath within thirty days of giving birth, while her husband was not with her. She caught cold, and her funeral bier was brought after Rava to Pumbedita.
shabbat-129a-8-8.why: Shmuel said a woman after childbirth has a thirty-day rule, which the Sages of Neharde'a read as a ban on immersing in that time because of the cold; Rava limits it to when her husband is away, and cites this incident.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage; his wife's death follows her immersion while he was away.

people.name: Rav Hisda's daughter
people.about: Rava's wife, who immersed within thirty days of childbirth and caught cold.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: Her father.

terms.meaning: Dipped in a ritual bath to become ritually pure, required of a woman after childbirth before marital relations resume.
The frame on which a body is carried to burial.

shabbat-129a-10-10.note: After bloodletting, Shmuel, Rav Yehuda and Rabba each needed a fire to keep warm. For Shmuel they broke up a teak armchair, for Rav Yehuda an ebony table, and for Rabba a bench, to use as fuel. Abaye asked Rabba whether breaking the bench did not violate the commandment 'Do not destroy'. Rabba answered that not destroying his own body mattered more to him.
shabbat-129a-10-10.why: Shmuel has ruled that a fire may be made on Shabbat for someone who let blood and caught cold, even in midsummer. These cases show how seriously the Sages took the danger of cold after bloodletting, even burning valuable furniture.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage for whom a teak armchair was broken up for a fire after bloodletting.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage for whom an ebony table was broken up for a fire.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: A Sage for whom a bench was broken up; he defended it to Abaye.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Rabba's student, who asked whether breaking the bench was wasteful destruction.

terms.meaning: Drawing blood from the body as a medical treatment, common in ancient times. The person was considered weakened and at risk afterward.
A Torah prohibition (Deuteronomy 20:19) against needlessly destroying useful or valuable things.

shabbat-129a-18-18.note: Ablat, a gentile scholar, found Shmuel lying in the sun. He asked him, Wise man of the Jews, can something harmful become good? Shmuel answered that on a day of bloodletting the sun is good for a person. The Gemara comments that this was not really so: there is one day in the year when the sun is beneficial, the day of the summer solstice, and Shmuel did not want to reveal that remedy to Ablat.
shabbat-129a-18-18.why: Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak has just advised that someone who let blood and has nothing to eat should lie in the sun. The story shows Shmuel doing so, and the Gemara adds that his stated reason was a cover.

people.name: Ablat
people.about: A gentile scholar who found Shmuel lying in the sun and questioned him.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage, called by Ablat the wise man of the Jews.

terms.meaning: Drawing blood from the body as a medical treatment; the person was considered weakened afterward and needed warmth and food.
The summer solstice, the longest day of the year, which falls around the Hebrew month of Tammuz.

shabbat-129a-22-22.note: Shmuel used to have blood let in a house whose walls were seven and a half bricks thick. One day after bloodletting he felt weak. He checked and found that a half-brick was missing from the wall.
shabbat-129a-22-22.why: Rav and Shmuel have just warned that someone who has blood let should not sit in the wind, lest it draw out more blood; this story shows even a small gap in a wall affecting Shmuel himself.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who felt weak after bloodletting and found a gap in the wall.

terms.meaning: Drawing blood from the body as a medical treatment, common in that era.

shabbat-130a-9-9.note: Levi visited the house of Yosef the hunter, where he was served a peacock's head cooked in milk. He did not eat it. When he later came before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, Rabbi asked him why he had not excommunicated the people of that house. Levi answered that the place was the home ground of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, and he thought that rabbi might have taught them to follow Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who allowed poultry with milk.
shabbat-130a-9-9.why: A teaching has just said that in Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's town people ate poultry with milk, following his view. This visit shows how the Sages treated a town that followed a local rabbi's lenient ruling.

people.name: Levi
people.about: A Sage who visited Yosef the hunter's house and refused the dish he was served.

people.name: Yosef the hunter
people.about: The host whose household served Levi a peacock's head in milk.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; he asked Levi why he had not excommunicated his hosts.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
people.about: The Sage whose locale it was; Levi thought he might have ruled leniently there.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
people.about: A Sage who held that eating poultry cooked in milk is permitted.

terms.meaning: To formally shun someone from the community, a penalty the Sages could impose on those who broke their rulings.
The Torah forbids cooking a kid in its mother's milk; most Sages extended this to poultry, but Rabbi Yosei HaGelili held that birds are not included.

shabbat-130a-11-11.note: Rabbi Yitzhak told of a city in the Land of Israel whose people followed Rabbi Eliezer's ruling on circumcision, doing even preparatory work for it on Shabbat. Its people died at their appointed time, not before. And once, when the wicked empire, Rome, issued a decree against the Jewish people forbidding circumcision, it did not issue the decree against that city.
shabbat-130a-11-11.why: The mishna quoted Rabbi Eliezer allowing even trees to be cut on Shabbat to make charcoal for circumcision tools, and a teaching said his town did so. Rabbi Yitzhak's account shows that town rewarded for its devotion to the commandment.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak
people.about: The Sage who tells of the city that followed Rabbi Eliezer.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A Sage who allowed the preparations for circumcision to be done on Shabbat.

terms.meaning: A baby boy is circumcised on his eighth day, even if it falls on Shabbat. The Sages argued over whether the preparations, like making the knife, may also be done on Shabbat.
The Land of Israel.

shabbat-130b-4-5.note: Rabbi Zeira had once asked Rabbi Asi a question about carrying in an alleyway, and Rabbi Asi had stayed silent. On another occasion Rabbi Zeira found him teaching a report: once people forgot to bring the circumcision knife before Shabbat and brought it on Shabbat, and the Rabbis were troubled that Rabbi Eliezer's view had been followed. Rabbi Oshaya added that the circumciser told him it was carried only from one end of an unmerged alleyway to the other. Rabbi Zeira asked whether Rabbi Asi now held that carrying there was allowed; he said yes. Asked why he had not said so before, he agreed that his knowledge had come back to him in the course of his studies.
shabbat-130b-4-5.why: Rabbi Zeira's earlier question, whether one may carry throughout an alleyway whose residents never merged, went unanswered. This later scene supplies Rabbi Asi's answer, which the Gemara then compares with Rav's ruling that such an alleyway allows carrying only four cubits.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A Sage who had asked Rabbi Asi a question earlier and found him teaching the answer later.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: A Sage who could not answer Rabbi Zeira at first, then later taught a case that answered it.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish
people.about: The Sage in whose name the report of the forgotten knife is told.

people.name: Rabbi Oshaya
people.about: A Sage who asked the circumciser where the knife was carried.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda the Cutter
people.about: A circumciser who told Rabbi Oshaya the knife was carried within an alleyway.

terms.meaning: Residents of courtyards opening onto a shared alleyway can pool food in a joint arrangement that lets them carry there on Shabbat. Here they had not done so.
A follower of the School of Shammai, whose views the law usually does not follow.
A rule that when one Sage disagrees with the majority, the law follows the majority.

shabbat-133b-17-17.note: When Rava taught the public in Mehoza how to make a bandage, the sons of Manyomei the doctor tore their clothes, since everyone could now treat themselves. Rava told them he had left them one cure to profit from: Shmuel said that one who washes his face and does not dry it well will get sores, and the remedy is to wash a great deal in water in which beets have been boiled.
shabbat-133b-17-17.why: The mishna allows a bandage on a circumcision wound on Shabbat, and Rava has just given the recipe for a bandage, wax and tree sap. This story tells what happened when he taught that recipe in public.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who taught a bandage recipe in Mehoza.

people.name: Manyomei the doctor
people.about: A doctor whose sons were upset that Rava gave away a cure.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage whose teaching about face sores Rava passed on to the doctor's sons.

terms.meaning: A traditional sign of grief or distress.

shabbat-134a-3-3.note: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar told how Rabbi Meir once had stomach pain on Shabbat, and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and those with him wanted to mix wine and oil for him. He would not let them. They asked whether his own ruling would be cancelled in his lifetime. He answered that although he held his view and his colleagues held theirs, he had never in his life dared to go against his colleagues' words. The Gemara concludes that he was strict only with himself.
shabbat-134a-3-3.why: A teaching cites Rabbi Meir as allowing wine and oil to be mixed for a sick person on Shabbat. This incident seems to show him refusing it, and the Gemara reads it so that the permission still stands for everyone else.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
people.about: The Sage who tells the story; he was among those who wanted to treat Rabbi Meir.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A Sage who allowed mixing wine and oil for the sick but refused it for himself.

terms.meaning: A remedy for the sick. The Sages forbade preparing medicines on Shabbat, and argued over whether this mixture counts.

shabbat-134a-14-14.note: Rabbi Natan told how, on a visit to the coastal cities, a woman came to him who had circumcised her first son and he died, and her second son and he died. She brought her third son to him. He saw the baby was red and told her to wait until the blood was absorbed into him. She waited, then circumcised him, and he lived. People called the boy Natan the Babylonian, after him.
shabbat-134a-14-14.why: Abaye has just quoted his foster mother: a baby who is red has not yet absorbed his blood, so his circumcision should wait. Rabbi Natan's account is brought as the source for that advice.

people.name: Rabbi Natan
people.about: A Sage, called the Babylonian, who advised a mother to delay her son's circumcision.

people.name: Natan the Babylonian
people.about: The name given to the baby who lived, after Rabbi Natan.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the era of the Mishna that was not included in the Mishna itself.

shabbat-134a-15-15.note: Rabbi Natan told of a second visit, to Cappadocia. Again a woman whose first two sons had died after circumcision brought her third son to him. He saw that the baby was pale and could find in him no blood of the covenant. He told her to wait until blood came into him. She waited, circumcised him, and he lived, and he too was called Natan the Babylonian after him.
shabbat-134a-15-15.why: Abaye has quoted his foster mother that a pale baby should not be circumcised until his blood comes into him. This second account of Rabbi Natan's supports that half of her advice, as the first account supported the advice about a red baby.

people.name: Rabbi Natan
people.about: A Sage who advised a mother in Cappadocia to delay circumcising her pale baby.

people.name: Natan the Babylonian
people.about: The name given to the baby who lived, after Rabbi Natan.

terms.meaning: The blood drawn at circumcision, which is called the covenant between God and Abraham's descendants.

shabbat-134b-8-9.note: A man came before Rava with a question about washing a newly circumcised baby, and Rava gave him the ruling he himself held. Afterward Rava fell ill and said: Why did I set myself against the views of the Elders? The Sages said to him that a teaching supported his view. He answered that the wording of the mishna fits theirs.
shabbat-134b-8-9.why: The Gemara has a baraita that matches Rava's reading of the mishna on when a circumcised baby may be washed on Shabbat. The story shows Rava himself backing away from it in favor of the Elders' stricter reading.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who ruled on washing a baby, fell ill, and regretted contradicting the Elders.

terms.meaning: Earlier Sages whose ruling on washing a baby was stricter than Rava's. The translation names them as Rav Yehuda and Rabba bar Avuh.
The core legal text of rabbinic law, compiled around 200 CE, on which the Gemara comments.

shabbat-135a-6-7.note: A son was born to Rav Adda bar Ahava already circumcised. He went around to thirteen circumcisers, and in the end the child was left with a severed urethra. Rav Adda said: I deserved this, because I went against Rav's ruling. Rav Nahman asked him: And did you not go against Shmuel's too? Shmuel required drawing a drop of blood only on a weekday, not on Shabbat. The Gemara explains that Rav Adda held such a child certainly has a hidden foreskin.
shabbat-135a-6-7.why: The Gemara has just stated a dispute: Rav said a baby born circumcised needs nothing done, while Shmuel said a drop of covenant blood must be drawn. Rav Adda's son shows what came of acting against Rav, and Rav Nahman's question turns to whether this may be done on Shabbat.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Ahava
people.about: A Sage whose son was born circumcised and was injured when the boy was circumcised.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage who ruled that a baby born circumcised needs no further cutting.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage who required drawing a drop of blood from a baby born circumcised.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A Sage who asked Rav Adda whether he had gone against Shmuel too.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: A Sage who held there is only a doubt that such a baby has a hidden foreskin.

terms.meaning: A baby born without a visible foreskin. The Sages debated whether a drop of blood must still be drawn as a sign of the covenant.
A foreskin present but hidden under the skin, which would mean the baby still needs a real circumcision.
An injury to the urinary passage, here caused by a botched circumcision.

shabbat-136a-17-17.note: A baby born to the son of Rav Dimi bar Yosef died within thirty days of birth, and the father sat in mourning for him. His own father, Rav Dimi bar Yosef, asked him whether he only wanted the special foods given to mourners. The son answered that he was certain the baby had been carried to full term.
shabbat-136a-17-17.why: The Gemara is discussing whether a baby who dies within thirty days counts as having been born viable, as Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel held. This father explains why he mourns anyway: he knew the pregnancy was full term.

people.name: Rav Dimi bar Yosef
people.about: A Sage who questioned his son for mourning a baby who died within thirty days.

people.name: son of Rav Dimi bar Yosef
people.about: A father who mourned his baby and said he knew the child was full term.

terms.meaning: A baby who dies before thirty days may be treated as never having been viable, so the usual mourning rites need not apply.
Mourners are served a meal by others. Rav Dimi suggests his son mourns only to get it.

shabbat-136a-18-18.note: Rav Ashi visited the house of Rav Kahana, whose child died within thirty days of birth. Rav Ashi saw Rav Kahana sitting in mourning for him and asked whether he did not follow Shmuel's ruling, as reported by Rav Yehuda, that the law follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. Rav Kahana answered that he was certain the child had been carried to full term.
shabbat-136a-18-18.why: The Gemara is discussing whether a baby who dies within thirty days counts as viable. This second account of a parent mourning such a baby gives the same answer as the one before it: a full-term birth is treated differently.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage who visited Rav Kahana and questioned his mourning.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: A Sage whose baby died within thirty days and who mourned him.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage who ruled that the law follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: A Sage who held that a baby who has not lived thirty days may be treated as never viable.

terms.meaning: A baby who dies before thirty days may be treated as never having been viable, so the usual mourning rites need not apply.

shabbat-139a-14-15.note: The people of Bashkar sent three questions to Levi: may a canopy be spread on Shabbat, are hops in a vineyard a forbidden mixture of crops, and what is done when someone dies on a Festival. While the messenger was on the way, Levi died. Shmuel told Rav Menashya to answer them if he was wise enough. Rav Menashya wrote that they had examined every side of the canopy question and found no way to permit it.
shabbat-139a-14-15.why: The Gemara returns to the law of a canopy on Shabbat. Afterward it asks why Rav Menashya hid the lenient views that existed, and answers that the people of Bashkar were not learned enough to apply them safely.

people.name: Levi
people.about: A Sage to whom the people of Bashkar sent questions; he died before they arrived.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage who told Rav Menashya to answer the questions.

people.name: Rav Menashya
people.about: The Sage who sent answers to the people of Bashkar.

terms.meaning: A tent-like covering over a bed. Spreading one on Shabbat can count as building a tent, which is forbidden.
The Torah forbids sowing other crops in a vineyard; the question was whether hops count.
A biblical holy day, such as Passover, on which most work is forbidden, as on Shabbat.

shabbat-139a-21-21.note: Rabbi Yehuda bar Sheilat reported in Rabbi Asi's name an incident in the synagogue of Maon on a Festival next to Shabbat. Someone died; he did not know whether the Festival fell before Shabbat or after it. They came before Rabbi Yohanan, who told them to let gentiles attend to the burial.
shabbat-139a-21-21.why: Rav Menashya had told the people of Bashkar that neither Jews nor gentiles may bury a body on a Festival. The Gemara cites this ruling of Rabbi Yohanan to challenge him, then explains he was strict because they were not learned.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda bar Sheilat
people.about: A Sage who passed on the report in Rabbi Asi's name.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: The Sage who told of the incident at Maon.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage who ruled that gentiles may bury the dead person on the Festival.

terms.meaning: A holy day falling on the day before or after Shabbat, so that two days of rest run together and burial would be put off.
A biblical holy day on which most work is forbidden.

shabbat-140a-9-9.note: Rav Yosef said that once he followed Mar Ukva into a bathhouse. When he came out, Mar Ukva gave him one cup of this wine drink, and he felt its chill from the hair on his head to the nails of his feet. Had he been given a second cup, he said, he would have feared that it would use up his reward in the World to Come. The Gemara asks how Mar Ukva drank it every day, and answers that he was used to it.
shabbat-140a-9-9.why: A teaching has just said that aluntit, a drink of aged wine, water and balsam taken after the bathhouse, may not be prepared on Shabbat because it is a remedy. Rav Yosef's experience shows how strong a drink it was.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: A Sage who tasted the cooling bathhouse drink.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: A Sage who gave Rav Yosef the drink and took it himself every day.

terms.meaning: The reward of the righteous after this life. Rav Yosef feared a second cup of pleasure would be paid out of it.
A drink of aged wine, clear water and balsam, taken to cool down after the bathhouse.

shabbat-140a-16-17.note: Rav Aha bar Yosef had heaviness of the heart. Mar Ukva told him to drink asafoetida over three days. He drank on Thursday and Friday, then on Shabbat morning asked in the study hall what to do. They told him a person may drink it on Shabbat without concern. He said his question was about soaking it, not drinking it. Rav Hiyya bar Avin said the same thing had happened to him: Rav Adda bar Ahava had no answer, and Rav Huna said that Rav's view was to soak it in cold water and set it in the sun.
shabbat-140a-16-17.why: The Gemara has just reported Rabbi Yannai ruling that soaking asafoetida even in cold water is forbidden. This case of a patient mid-treatment brings Rav's lenient ruling, which the Gemara then says could hold even for Rabbi Yannai, because stopping would endanger him.

people.name: Rav Aha bar Yosef
people.about: A Sage with heaviness of the heart who asked about preparing his remedy on Shabbat.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: A Sage who prescribed the asafoetida treatment.

people.name: Rav Hiyya bar Avin
people.about: A Sage who had faced the same question and reported the answer.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Ahava
people.about: A Sage who could not answer Rav Hiyya bar Avin's question.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage who answered in Rav's name: soak it in cold water and set it in the sun.

terms.meaning: A strong-smelling plant resin, soaked in water and drunk as a remedy.
An ailment felt as pain or pressure in the chest.
A measure of volume, a few liters.
The place where the Sages and their students learned together and answered questions.

shabbat-140b-17-17.note: Rav Hisda held a pearl in one hand and a clod of earth in the other while teaching his daughters. He showed them the pearl straight away. The clod he did not show them until they grew upset with curiosity, and only then did he show it.
shabbat-140b-17-17.why: Rav Hisda has been advising his daughters to be modest before their husbands. The Gemara presents this demonstration as his lesson in that modesty, in which what is hidden draws more interest than what is on display.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: A Sage who gave advice to his daughters and showed them a pearl and a clod of earth.

shabbat-142b-15-17.note: Abaye would put a spoon on bundles of produce so he could move them on Shabbat, and Rava would put a knife on a slaughtered young dove and move it. Rav Yosef mocked them: how sharp is the law of children! The Sages allowed this only for someone who forgot, not to be planned in advance. Abaye answered that the bundles could anyway be leaned on, and he used the spoon only because he was an important person. Rava said the same: the dove was fit to eat raw, so the knife was needed only because he was an important person.
shabbat-142b-15-17.why: The Gemara has quoted rulings that a forgotten object may be moved on Shabbat by setting bread or a baby on it, and Rav Ashi limited this. These Sages using the trick on purpose bring the question of when it is allowed.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who put a spoon on bundles of produce to move them on Shabbat.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who put a knife on a slaughtered young dove to move it.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: A Sage who mocked their practice as the law of children.

terms.meaning: From the outset, as a planned first choice, as against a fix after the fact.
A respected Sage, expected to be stricter in public so that others do not learn the wrong lesson from him.

shabbat-145b-9-10.note: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Asi sat before Rabbi Yohanan while he dozed. Rabbi Hiyya asked a string of questions: why are the birds of Babylonia fat, its Festivals joyous, its Torah scholars marked by their dress, and gentiles contaminated? Rabbi Asi had a quick answer for each. Rabbi Yohanan woke and scolded them: children, only say what is as clear to you as the fact that your sister is forbidden to you. When they asked him to answer, he said the birds of Babylonia are fat because they were never exiled, as a verse about Moab shows.
shabbat-145b-9-10.why: The mishna mentioned the kolyas, a fish from Spain, and Rabbi Abba's chicken from the Land of Israel, and the Gemara has been comparing Babylonian and Israeli food and tastes. This exchange turns to the differences between the two lands.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba
people.about: A Sage who asked questions about Babylonia while Rabbi Yohanan dozed.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: A Sage who gave quick answers to Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba's questions.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Their teacher, who woke, rebuked their guessing, and began to answer himself.

terms.term: Say to wisdom: You are my sister
terms.meaning: A verse from Proverbs, read by Rabbi Yohanan to mean that one should teach only what one knows as surely as one knows a sister is forbidden in marriage.
The land in what is now Iraq, home to a large Jewish community and its own academies of Sages.

shabbat-147a-1-1.note: Ulla came to Pumbedita and saw the rabbis there shaking dust from their cloaks on Shabbat. He said: The Rabbis are desecrating Shabbat. Rav Yehuda told the rabbis to go on shaking their cloaks in front of him, because in their place people were not at all particular about this.
shabbat-147a-1-1.why: Rav Huna has just ruled that shaking dust from a cloak on Shabbat counts as laundering, but only for new black garments whose owner is particular about them. This story shows the last condition in practice.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: A visiting Sage who objected to the rabbis of Pumbedita shaking their cloaks.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who told the rabbis they could keep shaking their cloaks in Ulla's presence.

terms.meaning: Doing work forbidden on the Sabbath.
Caring about keeping a garment clean. The Gemara rules that shaking off dust is forbidden only for someone who does care.

shabbat-147a-2-2.note: Abaye was standing before Rav Yosef, who asked him for his hat. Abaye saw there was dew on it and hesitated to hand it over. Rav Yosef told him to shake it off and throw it to him, since they were not at all particular about this.
shabbat-147a-2-2.why: Rav Huna has ruled that shaking a garment on Shabbat counts as laundering only if the owner is particular about keeping it clean. Like the story of Ulla in Pumbedita before it, this one shows that rule in practice.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A student who hesitated to hand Rav Yosef a hat with dew on it.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Abaye's teacher, who told him to shake off the dew and throw him the hat.

terms.meaning: Caring about keeping a garment clean. Shaking off dust or dew on Shabbat is forbidden only for someone who does care.

shabbat-147a-5-5.note: Rabbi Yehuda tells of Hyrcanus, son of Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus, who went out on Shabbat with a scarf on his shoulder and a thread of it tied around his finger so it would not fall. When the case came before the Sages, they said one may go out this way even without the thread tied to the finger. Rav Nahman bar Rav Hisda taught in the name of Rav Hisda that this is the law.
shabbat-147a-5-5.why: The Gemara has been sorting ways of wearing cloth over the shoulders on Shabbat: a folded cloak counts as carrying, while runners may wear scarves. This incident settles that a scarf on the shoulder counts as worn even when it is not tied down.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident.

people.name: Hyrcanus
people.about: Son of Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus; he went out with a scarf on his shoulder on Shabbat.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus
people.about: Father of Hyrcanus.

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Rav Hisda
people.about: Taught the ruling in the name of Rav Hisda.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: The Sage in whose name the final ruling is taught.

terms.meaning: The Sabbath. One of its prohibitions is carrying objects in a public area; clothing that is worn does not count as carried.
The binding Jewish law, as opposed to an opinion that was not accepted.

shabbat-147a-8-9.note: Rav Dimi reported that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi once went out into a field with both sides of his cloak resting on his shoulders. Yehoshua ben Zeiruz, son of Rabbi Meir's father-in-law, said to him: didn't Rabbi Meir hold one liable to a sin-offering for this? Rabbi asked whether Rabbi Meir was really that exacting, and lowered his cloak. Ravin gave another version: the man was Yehoshua ben Kefusai, Rabbi Akiva's son-in-law, citing Rabbi Akiva, and Rabbi lowered his cloak. Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yehuda said the report was that Rabbi was asked about it, not that he wore it so.
shabbat-147a-8-9.why: The Gemara is working out which ways of folding and draping a garment on Shabbat count as wearing it and which count as carrying; here the top Sage of his day gives way at once to a stricter view he had not known.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; he wore his cloak over his shoulders and lowered it when told of a stricter view.

people.name: Yehoshua ben Zeiruz
people.about: Son of Rabbi Meir's father-in-law; in Rav Dimi's version, he raised the objection.

people.name: Yehoshua ben Kefusai
people.about: Rabbi Akiva's son-in-law; in Ravin's version, he raised the objection.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: Brought the first version of the story from the Land of Israel to Babylonia.

people.name: Ravin
people.about: Brought a second version, naming a different questioner.

terms.meaning: A Temple sacrifice brought by someone who broke a serious law by mistake. Saying one is liable to it means the act counts as a real Shabbat violation.
Used alone as a name, it means Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, compiler of the Mishna.

shabbat-147b-4-4.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi recalled that when he and his fellow students learned Torah with Rabbi Shimon in Tekoa, they would carry oil and towels from the courtyard to the roof, and from the roof into an enclosure, until they reached the spring where they bathed. The Gemara adds the rulings of Shmuel and Rabbi Yohanan that one may dry oneself with a towel and carry it home.
shabbat-147b-4-4.why: Abaye asked Rav Yosef whether one may carry a towel home after bathing on Shabbat, and Rav Yosef named four authorities who allow it. The Gemara gives each one's source, and Rabbi's memory of Tekoa is his.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Tells of his student days, carrying towels to the spring.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's teacher in Tekoa; he allows carrying a towel home after drying off.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Ruled that one may dry off with a towel and carry it home.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Ruled the same, as reported by Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core code of Jewish law.
A fenced area, such as a yard, where carrying on Shabbat may be allowed, unlike a public street.

shabbat-147b-10-10.note: Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh came to Phrygia and Deyomset, was drawn after their wine and baths, and forgot his learning. When he returned and stood to read from a Torah scroll, he meant to read 'This month shall be for you' but read 'Have their hearts become deaf', mixing up look-alike Hebrew letters. The Sages prayed for mercy on him, and his learning was restored.
shabbat-147b-10-10.why: Rabbi Helbo has just said that the wine of Phrygia and the waters of Deyomset cost Israel the ten tribes. This story shows the same pull on one great Sage, and the Gemara then ties it to Rabbi Nehorai's advice to go into exile to a place of Torah.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh
people.about: A Sage who forgot his learning among the pleasures of Phrygia and Deyomset.

terms.meaning: A place of warm healing baths, mentioned alongside the wine region of Phrygia.
The handwritten scroll of the Five Books of Moses read aloud in the synagogue; it has no vowels, so the reader must know the text well.

shabbat-148a-0-0.note: Rabba bar bar Hana came to Pumbedita and did not attend Rav Yehuda's lecture. Rav Yehuda sent his attendant Adda to drag him there, and Adda did. Rabba bar bar Hana found Rav Yehuda teaching that one may not reset a broken bone on Shabbat, and told him that Rav Hana of Baghdad said in Shmuel's name that one may. Rav Yehuda answered: Hana is one of ours and Shmuel is one of ours, yet I had not heard this. Was I not right to drag you here?
shabbat-148a-0-0.why: The mishna forbids resetting a broken bone on Shabbat, and Shmuel rules that one may. The story shows that ruling arriving in Rav Yehuda's study hall, and the Gemara later uses it in a debate about a dislocated hand.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: A visitor to Pumbedita, dragged to Rav Yehuda's lecture, who brought Shmuel's ruling.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The teacher in Pumbedita whose lecture Rabba bar bar Hana skipped.

people.name: Adda
people.about: Rav Yehuda's attendant, sent to drag the visitor in.

people.name: Rav Hana of Baghdad
people.about: Reported Shmuel's ruling that a break may be reset on Shabbat.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage whose ruling permits resetting a broken bone on Shabbat.

terms.meaning: The binding Jewish law.
A Babylonian town with a major center of Torah study.

shabbat-150b-3-3.note: The Sages taught of a pious man whose field had a breach in its fence. He decided to fence it in, then remembered that it was Shabbat, so he held back and did not repair it. A miracle happened: a caper bush grew up in the gap, and from it came the livelihood of him and his household.
shabbat-150b-3-3.why: The mishna forbids waiting at the Shabbat boundary for nightfall in order to start weekday work, and the discussion has been about which weekday plans one may make or speak of on Shabbat. The pious man would not act even on a thought of work formed on Shabbat.

terms.meaning: A person who goes beyond what the law requires in serving God.
A thorny shrub whose buds and berries are eaten; here it closes the gap like a living fence.

shabbat-151b-1-1.note: Rav Yehuda reports in Shmuel's name that a student of Rabbi Meir followed him into the bathhouse on Shabbat. The student wanted to rinse the floor, and Rabbi Meir told him one may not rinse. He wanted to smear the floor with oil, and Rabbi Meir told him one may not smear.
shabbat-151b-1-1.why: The mishna allows rinsing a corpse and smearing it with oil on Shabbat. The Gemara raises this incident as a challenge and answers that one floor can be confused with another, so the Sages forbade it, but a corpse cannot be confused with the ground.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: Stopped his student from rinsing and oiling the bathhouse floor on Shabbat.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Reports the incident in the name of Shmuel.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage in whose name the incident is told.

shabbat-151b-13-13.note: Rabbi Hiyya told his wife: when a poor person comes, be quick to give him bread, so that others will be quick to give bread to your children. She said: are you cursing them? He answered that a verse is written, 'Due to this thing', and the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught that it means a wheel that turns in the world. The Gemara adds Rabbi Gamliel's teaching that whoever has compassion for others receives compassion from Heaven.
shabbat-151b-13-13.why: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar has just taught that poverty comes round to every family in time, reading the same verse as a turning wheel. Rabbi Hiyya puts that teaching into practice in his own home.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: Tells his wife to give bread to the poor quickly.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya's wife
people.about: Asks whether he is cursing their children.

people.name: Rabbi Gamliel
people.about: Son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi; taught that compassion for others brings compassion from Heaven.

terms.meaning: The students and tradition of the Sage Rabbi Yishmael, quoted as a source of teachings.

shabbat-151b-16-16.note: When Rabbi Hanina's daughter died, he did not cry over her. His wife asked him whether he had merely let a chicken out of the house. He answered that if he cried he would suffer twice: from the loss and from blindness. The Gemara explains that he followed a teaching that some tears are bad for the eyes, among them tears of crying out of grief.
shabbat-151b-16-16.why: The discussion has just cited Shmuel's statement that after age forty, tears permanently weaken the eyesight. Rabbi Hanina's refusal to weep for his daughter puts that belief into practice.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: A Sage who did not weep when his daughter died, for fear of losing his sight.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage who reported the teaching about good and bad tears.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei ben Ketzarta
people.about: The Sage in whose name Rabbi Yohanan taught that there are six kinds of tears.

shabbat-152a-3-5.note: A certain eunuch, an apostate, taunted Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa, who was bald, by asking how far it was to 'Karḥina', a pun on baldness. The rabbi answered with a pun on castration, and they traded jibes about a bald buck and a castrated goat. Seeing the rabbi without shoes, the eunuch said a man with no horse, no donkey and no shoes is worse off than the buried dead. The rabbi replied that the glory of a face is a beard, the joy of the heart is a wife, and children are God's portion, and blessed is God who denied the eunuch all three. The eunuch asked: does a bald man quarrel? The rabbi asked: does a castrated goat rebuke?
shabbat-152a-3-5.why: The Gemara is expounding Ecclesiastes' verses on old age and has quoted the Sages' sayings about aging bodies; it adds this exchange of insults about bodily defects before returning to old age.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa
people.about: A bald Sage, taunted by the eunuch, who gives as good as he gets

terms.meaning: A Jew who has abandoned the Jewish faith.
A castrated man, who cannot grow a beard or father children.
A coin; the jibes compare the price of a bald goat and a castrated one.

shabbat-152a-15-15.note: Rav Yehuda taught that when a dead person has no one to mourn him, ten people should go and sit in his place. A man died in Rav Yehuda's neighborhood with no mourners, so every day of the seven days of mourning Rav Yehuda brought ten people to sit in the man's house. After seven days the dead man appeared to Rav Yehuda in a dream and said: put your mind at rest, for you have put my mind at rest.
shabbat-152a-15-15.why: Rav Hisda has just taught that a person's soul mourns for him all seven days after death; the story shows the dead are aware of those who mourn them, and Rabbi Abbahu goes on to say the dead know what is said before them.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Brought ten people each day to sit in mourning for a neighbor who had no mourners.

people.name: the dead man
people.about: A neighbor of Rav Yehuda with no mourners, who thanks him in a dream.

terms.meaning: Here, mourners: the family members who sit at home after a death and receive visitors who come to console them.
The first week of mourning after a burial, when mourners stay home and are visited.

shabbat-152b-8-11.note: Diggers working Rav Nahman's land were rebuked by Rav Ahai bar Yoshiya, who was buried there. They told Rav Nahman a man had rebuked them. Rav Nahman asked who he was; he said: Ahai bar Yoshiya. Rav Nahman asked: didn't Rav Mari say the righteous will turn to dust? Ahai: who is Mari, whom I do not know? Rav Nahman cited the verse 'And the dust returns to the earth'. Ahai answered that whoever taught him Ecclesiastes did not teach him Proverbs: 'envy is the rotting of the bones', so one without envy does not rot. Rav Nahman touched him, found him solid, and invited him into his house. Ahai said he had not read the Prophets either, citing 'when I open your graves'. To 'dust you are', Ahai replied it applies an hour before the resurrection.
shabbat-152b-8-11.why: Rav Mari has just said that even the bodies of the righteous will become dust. In this story a dead Sage, his body whole, argues back against that very statement.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The landowner who questions the dead man found on his land.

people.name: Rav Ahai bar Yoshiya
people.about: Buried in Rav Nahman's land; his body has not decayed, and he answers from the grave.

people.name: Rav Mari
people.about: The Sage who taught that the righteous turn to dust.

terms.meaning: Parts of the Hebrew Bible. Ahai mocks Rav Nahman for knowing one book but not the others.
The belief that God will one day bring the dead back to life.

shabbat-154b-7-7.note: Rabban Gamliel's donkey was loaded with honey on Shabbat, and he would not unload it until Shabbat was over. When Shabbat ended, the donkey died.
shabbat-154b-7-7.why: The mishna lets one take movable items off an animal on Shabbat, so the Gemara asks why Rabban Gamliel did not. It answers that the honey had spoiled, which made it off-limits to handle, and then asks why he let the animal suffer.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Would not unload his donkey's honey on Shabbat, and the donkey died.

shabbat-156b-1-2.note: Shmuel and the gentile sage Ablet were sitting and watching people go to the lake. Ablet said one man would not come back, because a snake would bite him and he would die. Shmuel said: if he is a Jew, he will go and come back. He went and came back. Ablet threw down the man's load and found inside a snake cut in two. Shmuel asked him what he had done. He said his group pooled bread every day; that day one of them had none and was embarrassed, so he offered to collect it and, at that man's turn, pretended to take from him. Shmuel said: you did a mitzva, and taught that 'charity saves from death' means even from death itself.
shabbat-156b-1-2.why: The Gemara is arguing that there is no constellation for the Jewish people: the fate written in the stars does not bind them. After deriving this from Abraham, it brings Shmuel's story as further proof.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage who predicts the man will return, and draws the lesson about charity.

people.name: Ablet
people.about: A gentile sage who foretells the man's death by snakebite.

terms.meaning: The arrangement of stars and planets at a person's birth, believed by astrologers to fix his fate.
A commandment or good deed done in obedience to God.

shabbat-156b-3-4.note: Chaldean astrologers told Rabbi Akiva that on the day his daughter entered the wedding canopy, a snake would bite her and she would die. She worried greatly. That day she stuck her hair pin into the wall, and it happened to go into the eye of a snake. In the morning, when she pulled the pin out, the snake came out with it. Her father asked what she had done. She said a poor man had knocked at the door that evening while everyone was busy with the feast, and no one heard him, so she took her own portion and gave it to him. Rabbi Akiva said: you did a mitzva, and taught that 'charity saves from death' means even from death itself.
shabbat-156b-3-4.why: The Gemara is proving that there is no constellation for the Jewish people, that the stars' decree does not bind them; this is the next proof after Shmuel's story of the man saved from a snake.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The father, warned by astrologers about his daughter; he draws the lesson about charity.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva's daughter
people.about: Foretold to die on her wedding day; she is saved after giving her meal to a poor man.

terms.meaning: Astrologers; the name of an ancient people famous for reading the stars.
The canopy under which a Jewish wedding takes place; entering it means getting married.
A commandment or good deed done in obedience to God.

shabbat-156b-5-5.note: Chaldean astrologers told the mother of Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak that her son would be a thief. She never let him go with his head uncovered, telling him: cover your head so that the fear of Heaven will be upon you, and pray for mercy. He did not know why she said this. One day he was sitting and studying under a palm tree when his cloak fell off his head. He looked up, saw the palm tree, was overcome by his urge, climbed up and bit off a cluster of dates with his teeth.
shabbat-156b-5-5.why: This is the last of the Gemara's proofs that there is no constellation for the Jewish people, that fate in the stars does not bind them: the forecast came true only in the moment the head covering slipped.

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak
people.about: A Sage whose birth was said to mark him as a thief.

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak's mother
people.about: Kept her son's head covered after astrologers' warning.

terms.meaning: Astrologers; the name of an ancient people famous for reading the stars.
Awe of God; covering the head is a sign of it.
